text:
Heart Attack (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When the heart no longer goes along with a life that has long been lived past it.
Definition: A heart attack (myocardial infarction) refers to the acute death of heart-muscle tissue, usually caused by a blocked coronary artery, resulting in an insufficient supply of oxygen and nutrients (ischemia). The trigger is typically coronary artery disease (CAD) – a progressive narrowing of the coronary arteries caused by atherosclerosis, i.e. deposits (plaques) on the vessel walls. If such a plaque ruptures, a blood clot (thrombus) can form that completely blocks the vessel.
Typical symptoms: Sudden, often crushing pressure or pain behind the breastbone lasting longer than 5 minutes; Pain radiating into the left arm, both arms, jaw, neck, back, or upper abdomen; Shortness of breath, even without physical exertion; Cold sweat, nausea, vomiting; A sense of impending doom, strong inner distress; In women, older adults, and diabetics, symptoms are often less typical: a diffuse feeling of pressure, exhaustion, or nausea instead of classic chest pain – no less common, but easier to miss
Emergency notice: If you suspect an acute heart attack (e.g. sudden, persistent pressure or pain in the chest, radiating into the arm, jaw or back, shortness of breath, cold sweat, a sense of impending doom): call emergency services immediately, request an ambulance, or go to the nearest hospital without delay. In this situation every minute counts – this is not the moment for psychosomatic interpretation, but for immediate emergency medical care.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Cardiology has known since the 1950s the concept of the „Type A personality“ (Friedman & Rosenman): ambitious, time-driven, competitive, with suppressed or explosive aggression – a pattern that long-term studies correlate with elevated cardiovascular risk. Traditional Chinese Medicine likewise assigns the heart to the Fire element, the seat of Shen, the spirit and the joy of life – when this fire falls out of rhythm, psychosomatic medicine often reads it as an expression of denied or forced joy, chronic self-overextension, or a life that has long been lived past one's own heart.
--- Type 1: Anger – the question of where it may go ---
SE1: In the self-preservation One, anger turns most radically inward: self-control becomes the supreme life principle, every impulse must be checked, justified, pressed into the corset of what is correct. A typical picture is the person who speaks in a calm voice even in acute rage, while everything vibrates inside – outward composure, inward a pressure cooker under permanent strain. Cardiologically this pattern is well studied: chronically suppressed hostility counts as one of the strongest psychological predictors of coronary events, even stronger than openly expressed anger, because the body is never granted a physiological release. The heart pumps against a resistance that may never be named as such.
SO1: The social One turns personal anger into a cause for the community – 'this makes me furious' becomes 'this is unjust and must change.' This translation protects against feeling selfish, but costs energy: the reformer carries not only her own outrage but the felt responsibility for the state of the whole world, without ever being finished. Unlike the self-preservation variant, the anger does find an outlet in words, petitions, engagement – but the strain works more through chronic cognitive exhaustion and the nagging sense of unresolved wrongs than through classic muscular tension. The heart wears itself out here less through pressure than through the sheer volume of what still needs fixing.
SX1: In the sexual One, anger discharges most directly where it hurts most – in intimacy: intense, demanding expectations of the partner, jealousy, the silent insistence on working toward a perfect relationship, whatever it takes. Small disappointments quickly become proof of insufficient devotion, and hurt turns into sharp criticism within seconds. This creates a more immediate outlet than in the other two One variants – potentially less silent, sustained tension, but instead an emotional rollercoaster with intense, episodic peaks of strain precisely in the moments that should offer the most safety.
--- Type 2: Pride – whose needs count ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two lives the sentence 'I need no one' most literally of all three variants: she cares practically, unobtrusively, often within the closest family circle – cooking, organizing, keeping things running – and would rather collapse than openly ask for help. The strain here arises not from competing for recognition but from a quiet, never-spoken imbalance: she covers for others without ever being covered herself. Her own heart – literally and figuratively – simply goes unheard for decades, because no one asks and she never demands it.
SO2: The social Two seeks her pride through public indispensability: she is the person in the club, the neighborhood, the office who is available for everything, who never says 'no,' because being needed is her strongest confirmation. Chronic overload arises here less from quiet self-denial in private than from the sheer number of obligations that accumulate unnoticed – a form of exhaustion close to so-called helper syndrome, which often only shows once literally no one is left to help her, while she helps everyone else.
SX2: The sexual Two seeks pride not through the many but through her one, irresistible effect on a single person – seduction, intense attention, a giving that can quickly turn possessive because her own significance hinges on this one bond. Emotional volatility, jealousy, and the constant, unspoken question 'am I still enough?' act here as an independent, standing stressor – cardiologically relevant less through classic overwork exhaustion than through the episodic but intense stress peaks of a relationship that never fully settles.
--- Type 3: Performance – where the heart keeps pace ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three measures her own worth by the nearest concrete result: the finished task, the neatly kept accounts, the garden that looks better than the neighbor's. She rarely shines in public – her confirmation comes through quiet, efficient busyness, often without anyone but herself noticing how much she achieves. Exhaustion is consistently reinterpreted: not as a warning sign but as a character weakness to be overcome. The heart keeps pumping to the rhythm of self-set targets long after the body has sent clear signals to slow down.
SO3: The social Three seeks success visibly and in comparison: career, titles, the car in the driveway, the audience's recognition. Of all 27 subtypes she comes closest to the classic cardiologically described Type A personality – ambitious, time-driven, in an inner race that never really ends, because the next comparison, the next competitor, the next personal best is already waiting. The heart works here against a clock that ticks only in her own head, but real enough to keep raising blood pressure and pulse permanently.
SX3: The sexual Three deploys her drive to perform specifically within the relationship: attractiveness, charisma, constant self-optimization, so as to be unsurpassed for the one important person – 'the best,' not in a competition, but in the eyes of the beloved. The exhaustion here arises less from public comparison than from the private, never-ending pressure to show no weakness, no lapse, no letting-up even in the most intimate sphere – a demand that costs the most strength exactly where relaxation should be possible.
--- Type 4: Envy – when longing rather than rage burdens the heart ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four, the counter-type among the Fours, rarely shows the expected dramatic suffering – she functions, cares, holds on, often for decades, while inside a deep, never-acknowledged longing for the real, authentic life runs alongside. The link to the heart-attack pattern lies here less in open rage than in chronically suppressed grief: a life that continues quietly and dutifully while much stays unspoken inside, settling on the heart as a silent, never-addressed burden.
SO4: The social Four carries her pain outward, speaks openly about exhaustion and overwhelm instead of hiding them behind a facade – this expression acts like a safety valve, taking at least part of the pressure off the heart that other subtypes' silent exhaustion accumulates unchecked. Cardiologically the strain still shows, but more in phases of pronounced exhaustion after emotional peaks than in the steady, chronically concealed tension the classic Type-A pattern describes.
SX4: The sexual Four lives uncompromising emotional intensity in the one relationship, often accompanied by a constant, tormenting comparison – with former partners, an imagined ideal, with what love could be but currently isn't. Fierce emotional swings and a potentially conflict-ridden, up-and-down relationship dynamic are the more likely strain factor here than quiet, sustained tension – the heart is stressed less by ongoing pressure than by recurring, intense emotional shocks.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal – when distance itself becomes the risk ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five systematically reduces her life to the essentials: minimal needs, minimal contact, a self-chosen, often pleasantly experienced withdrawal from a world felt as intrusive and energy-draining. In the classic sense this is not a Type-A pattern – the outward busyness is entirely absent. But social isolation is itself a well-documented, independent medical risk factor for cardiovascular disease, regardless of acute stress: a heart that rarely beats in exchange with others loses some of what demonstrably supports heart-rate variability and recovery.
SO5: The social Five seeks her place in the group through knowledge, not closeness – she observes, collects, comments from the sidelines, maintaining an inner distance even where she is physically present. This mix of participation and withdrawal means her own needs are rarely named clearly, because naming itself already feels too exposing – a quiet but steady form of self-denial that settles over the years into a body that has likewise learned to ask for little.
SX5: The sexual Five shares herself intensely, but exclusively with very few, carefully chosen people – an 'intimate' bond of great emotional depth, surrounded by radical shutting-out of everyone else. This concentration on a single or very few bonds can genuinely nourish, yet the near-total absence of a broader social network – likewise described medically as a cardiovascular risk factor – means that if this one bond is lost or withdrawn, almost no safety net remains.
--- Type 6: Fear – the body on permanent alert ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six meets the world with caution, forward planning, and an inner early-warning system that rarely truly switches off – reserves, contingency plans, mentally rehearsing what could go wrong before it even happens. This form of constant alertness is medically anything but harmless: chronically elevated cortisol and adrenaline levels from sustained vigilance count as a plausible mechanism for elevated cardiovascular risk, even when no concrete, nameable event ever occurs – the body reacts to the anticipation of danger almost as if it had already arrived.
SO6: The social Six seeks security not in her own precautions but in belonging – to a group, an institution, a clear authority she follows loyally and whose rules she conscientiously observes. The strain here arises chiefly from a felt responsibility for the collective: worry not primarily about herself, but about whether the community her own security depends on stays intact – a worry rarely voiced openly, settling instead as diffuse, chronic inner tension.
SX6: The sexual Six meets fear counterphobically: through projecting strength, deliberate provocation, actively seeking out exactly what she fears in order to disprove it rather than avoid it. This mix of fear and anger produces less an even, sustained tension than its own episodic strain peaks – intense moments of confrontation in which heart rate and blood pressure spike briefly but clearly, followed by phases of relative calm, until the next self-sought test of nerve.
--- Type 7: Excess – scattering instead of stillness ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven secures herself through a multitude of parallel options – several projects, several contacts, several possible escape routes should one of them not pay off. This practical hedging feels like freedom but produces its own kind of exhaustion: not through classic tension, but through sheer scattering, the constant jumping between possibilities without ever truly arriving at one. The heart experiences here less pressure than permanent overstimulation, a nervous system that rarely finds rest because another option is always beckoning.
SO7: The social Seven, the counter-type among Sevens, consistently sets aside her own needs in favor of others – an idealistic, often duty-bound self-sacrifice barely recognizable from outside as a Seven pattern, because the usual lightness is missing. Her own exhaustion is denied for a long time, often with the argument that others need it more urgently – until the body eventually presents a bill the alert mind long refused to see.
SX7: The sexual Seven lives boundless, impulsive enthusiasm, 'everything, now' – a lifestyle built on intensity rather than moderation. Here the more plausible link to heart-attack risk is often not the inner tension itself but the lived-out daily life: a heightened susceptibility to nicotine, alcohol, or other stimulants as ways to heighten her own intensity further – medically recognized, well-documented risk factors that arise here less from avoidance than from a fundamental too-much.
--- Type 8: Control – the strength that may never let up ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight secures her own existence through hard-nosed control over material and physical resources – money, possessions, physical strength, everything that guarantees independence. Withdrawal or admitting a need for rest are not experienced as legitimate human impulses but as an opening she may not allow herself. The heart runs permanently on high tension, because there is simply no room in the inner self-image for powering down – strength here means never appearing visibly tired.
SO8: The social Eight takes control not for herself but for the group, often in a self-appointed protector role: 'no one in my circle may be weak while I can be strong.' The pressure of responsibility and permanent leadership tension are the central strain factor here – a heart that must beat not only for its own safety but, felt as, for everyone else's, rarely finding a moment where it may simply be there for itself.
SX8: The sexual Eight lives total devotion and control in the one relationship, pure intensity, nothing half-hearted – every gesture, every conflict, every reconciliation is lived through with full force. The strain accordingly shows not as even, sustained tension but as extreme emotional and physical swings: short, highly intense phases in which pulse and blood pressure spike noticeably, followed by equally intense phases of closeness, in a rhythm that rarely knows moderation.
--- Type 9: Self-forgetting – the heart that was never heard ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine flees into comfort, fixed routines, and the consistent avoidance of any conflict – at first glance a picture of low acute stress. But 'self-forgetting' here means exactly what it says: her own heart's wishes go truly unheard for decades, neither by others nor by herself, because her own wanting is consistently subordinated to outward peace. This may be the most literal correspondence to this whole entry's core thesis – a life lived past its own heart for decades, without it ever being named as a loss.
SO9: The social Nine seeks harmony at any price within the group and subordinates her own opinion so consistently that eventually she barely knows what she actually thinks or wants herself. This chronic self-erasure for the sake of social peace looks from outside like adaptability, but costs considerably over the years: a heart that keeps giving up its own voice for the collective's sake loses exactly the clarity that self-care would require.
SX9: The sexual Nine merges with the partner so completely that her own identity dissolves into the other – not out of weakness, but as the deepest form of devotion native to this subtype. In its purest expression this may be the clearest version of a heart that never found its own, independent voice: not because it was silenced, but because it dissolved willingly, step by step, into the voice of the beloved, until barely any boundary remained perceptible between the two.
No subtype is immune to a heart attack, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes negotiates with the heart as the organ of life force in its own way – some through tension and control, others through withdrawal, exhaustion, or a need of their own that was never heard. This is exactly where this Compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outer symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance. When this life force – regardless of which of the 27 subtypes is affected – is brought back into balance, the symptom picture can resolve holistically, instead of merely being suppressed on the surface.

Atherosclerosis (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When, over decades, what was never allowed to flow settles and hardens.
Definition: Atherosclerosis (commonly known as „hardening of the arteries“) is a chronic condition of the artery walls that usually progresses over decades: fat, calcium, connective tissue and inflammatory cells build up as plaques inside the vessel wall, and the arteries gradually harden and narrow. Virtually any artery in the body can be affected – the coronary arteries (coronary artery disease), the vessels supplying the brain (stroke risk), or the leg arteries (peripheral arterial disease, „intermittent claudication“). Atherosclerosis itself is usually silent for years and often only becomes visible through its consequences – heart attack, stroke, circulatory disturbances.
Typical symptoms: Usually no noticeable symptoms for years – the disease stays silent for a long time; When leg arteries narrow: calf pain while walking that eases at rest (intermittent claudication); When coronary arteries narrow: pressure or pain in the chest under exertion (angina pectoris); When the vessels supplying the brain narrow: temporary visual disturbances, speech disturbances, weakness on one side of the body (warning signs of stroke); Cold feet, poorly healing wounds on the legs as a sign of advanced circulatory disturbance; Erectile dysfunction can be an early warning sign of atherosclerosis
Emergency notice: If symptoms appear suddenly – visual disturbances, speech disturbances, weakness or numbness on one side of the body, severe chest pain, or a sudden, severe loss of circulation in a leg – call emergency services immediately. These symptoms can indicate an acute stroke, heart attack, or vessel blockage – here every minute counts, this is not the moment for psychosomatic interpretation.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Conventional medicine today understands atherosclerosis primarily as a chronic inflammatory process: tiny injuries to the inner vessel wall, often promoted by high blood pressure, smoking, or elevated blood lipids, set off a years-long cascade of inflammation and deposit-building. Traditional Chinese Medicine describes a related picture as Blood stagnation (Xue Yu) – a flow that comes to a halt because Qi has been unable to circulate freely for a long time. Psychosomatic medicine often reads this slow, silent hardening of the vessels as a symbol: a life, an attitude, or a feeling that was no longer allowed to flow for decades, but instead solidified layer by layer – until the body itself becomes rigid where the soul already was.
--- Type 1: Anger that hardens into deposits ---
SE1: Nothing may show outwardly: the self-preservation One's anger stays internally managed, ordered, justified for decades. Typical is the person who still says a polite thank-you at the tenth slight in life, while an inner ledger has long been kept. Psychosomatic medicine reads this permanent management of tension that never finds real release as a plausible image for a process that deposits layer by layer in the vessel walls: not a single shock, but the silent, decades-long sum of countless small, never-resolved moments of tension.
SO1: An outlet in words, reform-mindedness, and the feeling of fighting for what's right is what the social One's anger finds when she turns it into moral engagement for the group. But the underlying sense that the world must be permanently corrected, that something somewhere is always wrong, remains a chronic, never fully resolved inner state of tension. Unlike the self-preservation variant, the burden here lies less in suppressed personal rage than in the sheer permanence of a fight that can never be finally won.
SX1: A sharp word, a disappointed look, the unmistakable statement when something doesn't match her expectations: this is how the sexual One lives out anger more directly, within the relationship itself. This creates potentially less silent, sustained hardening than in the other two variants, but recurring episodes of intense emotional tension in exactly the relationship that should be a refuge – episodes that can accumulate over the years, even though each one passes on its own.
--- Type 2: Pride that lets no one in ---
SE2: Literally nothing flows back, because she forbids herself to ask for anything in return: this is how the self-preservation Two suppresses her own needs for decades in favor of others. This one-sided, never-reciprocated flow reads psychosomatically as a direct image for vessels that narrow because the cycle of giving and receiving is out of balance across an entire lifespan: a system that permanently flows in only one direction eventually loses the elasticity healthy exchange requires.
SO2: Always available, never declining: this is how the social Two seeks meaning through permanent availability to the community, her self-worth hanging directly on being needed. The inability to say no thus produces a chronic overload that can condense over the years into a silent, sustained strain on the entire circulatory system – not through a dramatic moment, but through the sheer number of obligations that never truly exhausts itself, because there's always someone else who needs her.
SX2: Attention, care, the constant effort to be indispensable to the beloved: this is how the sexual Two invests intense, often possessive giving into the one relationship. Emotional volatility and jealousy act here more as episodic strain peaks than as even, sustained narrowing: phases of intense closeness alternate with phases of fear of not being enough, which stresses the vascular system in waves rather than under constant pressure.
--- Type 3: Performance that never interrupts the flow ---
SE3: Exhaustion is interpreted by the self-preservation Three as weakness, not as a signal to be taken seriously – she keeps working quietly and efficiently even when her body has long demanded a break. She is the person who uses her evening to finish the tax return while others relax, experiencing this not as being driven but as simple common sense. Over decades this constant self-overextension condenses into a picture in which the vessels, too, never come to rest – a system in permanent operation, lacking the recovery phases healthy vascular elasticity would require.
SO3: A life in constant competition mode that comes closest to the classic picture of the Type-A personality: this is how the social Three seeks success visibly and in comparison with others, knowing almost no real recovery phases for years. Every success is immediately relativized by the next possible comparison, every acknowledgment is valid only until someone else surpasses it – a state of permanent, self-generated alertness that gives the vascular system almost no chance to relax over the decades.
SX3: Attractiveness, adaptability, the constant readiness to reinvent herself for the one person – all of this costs the sexual Three energy that is rarely recognized as exhaustion, because it stays hidden behind the feeling of needing to be loved in order to be valuable. The pressure to never let up, even in the most intimate sphere, is rarely named openly, but is carried for years.
--- Type 4: Longing that settles in ---
SE4: Never in motion, only in inner hardening does the decades-long unspoken longing of the self-preservation Four discharge – the counter-type, who carries suffering tenaciously and barely visibly outward. She functions outwardly inconspicuous, almost brave, while inwardly a deep sense of being different, of not quite belonging, runs alongside, never given room to show itself or resolve. This silent carrying without an outlet fits the image of a deposit that hardens layer by layer, because it may never surface.
SO4: Where other subtypes hide their exhaustion, the social Four puts her vulnerability openly on display, making it almost part of her identity within the group – this showing is itself an outlet: the tension accumulates less because it regularly finds a way out. The underlying longing for wholeness nonetheless remains, even though here at least it gets voiced.
SX4: Nothing ever feels quite complete enough, always the suspicion lingers that it could be more intense, more real, deeper elsewhere: this is how the sexual Four lives uncompromising emotional intensity, often in constant comparison with ideals or other relationships. Fierce, episodic swings shape the picture here more than an even, silent hardening: the vessels experience less constant pressure than recurring, intense emotional waves.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that narrows the channels ---
SE5: Contact with others is experienced by the self-preservation Five as a cost, not as nourishment – she withdraws radically, reducing contact and needs to a sparse, self-sufficient life. Social isolation is itself a medically recognized risk factor for vascular disease, independent of acute stress, and thus fits especially clearly the picture of a system that narrows itself over the years: a circulatory system rarely activated through exchange with others loses something of its natural breadth.
SO5: Without ever truly being present, the social Five can shine in company, because part of her is always already back in the observer role – she seeks access to the group through knowledge but keeps an inner distance. This mix of participation and withdrawal means her own needs are rarely named clearly, because naming itself would already demand too much closeness – a quiet, chronic constriction that can settle into the system over the years.
SX5: Within one narrow but deep bond, with simultaneous radical shutting-out elsewhere, genuine exchange can indeed take place – this is how the sexual Five shares herself intensely but only with very few people, yet the near-total absence of a broader social network means the vascular system as a whole rarely benefits from the widening effect of diverse social contact.
--- Type 6: Fear that deposits layer by layer ---
SE6: Security is sought but never finally found, and the tension persists year after year – this is how the self-preservation Six's permanent alertness can plausibly be linked, via chronically elevated stress-hormone levels, to a heightened risk of vascular change. She plans for contingencies that never occur, and even when nothing happens, the relief lasts only briefly before the next worry takes hold.
SO6: As a steady sense of duty in the background, the responsibility for the collective that the social Six feels persists when she seeks security through belonging to a group or an authority. This loyalty costs energy over decades, because her own well-being is consistently set behind the community's.
SX6: To prove that fear does not control her, the sexual Six deliberately seeks out situations others would avoid, meeting fear counterphobically rather than with retreat – a pattern that produces intense but episodic rather than chronic tension.
--- Type 7: Excess that overtaxes the vessels ---
SE7: Restlessness and a lifestyle built on permanent scattering rather than rest count medically as an independent risk factor for vascular change – the self-preservation Seven hedges herself through options, networks, and indulgences, independent of inner tension. She always has a plan B, C, and D, and it is precisely this constant keeping-open of possibilities that prevents her from ever truly settling.
SO7: She cares for everyone except herself, only to be surprised when her body eventually sets limits: this is how the social Seven, the counter-type, sets her own needs aside in favor of others – an idealistic, often duty-bound self-sacrifice that denies her own exhaustion for a long time.
SX7: Regardless of how happy or unhappy this person feels, the appeal of intensity itself becomes a health risk when the sexual Seven lives boundless, impulsive enthusiasm: nicotine, alcohol, or other stimulants are recognized, medically well-documented risk factors for atherosclerosis here.
--- Type 8: Control that leaves no room ---
SE8: Experienced as an opening rather than a legitimate need, the self-preservation Eight's need for rest is set aside – she secures her own existence through control over material and physical resources. The system runs permanently on high tension, because powering down has no place in her inner self-image: whoever appears weak, the unspoken conviction goes, loses control over everything they fought for.
SO8: Not only her own burden, but also the felt responsibility for everyone else's well-being, is carried by the social Eight, who takes on responsibility and leadership for the group – permanent leadership tension and the conviction of never being allowed to be weak are the central, long-acting strain factor here.
SX8: Fought out with full force, conflict as much as reconciliation: this is how the sexual Eight lives total devotion and control in the one relationship, pure intensity, nothing half-hearted – a rhythm that leaves little room for calm in-between tones.
--- Type 9: Self-forgetting that hardens silently ---
SE9: Little visible tension outwardly, but a decades-long, continued self-forgetting in which her own needs are never heard: this is how the self-preservation Nine flees into comfort, routine, and conflict avoidance. This exact silent hardening may fit most directly the picture of a disease that itself stays symptom-free for years: both develop hidden, without anyone – including the person herself – really looking.
SO9: Out of fear of causing unrest, the social Nine rarely says what she really thinks, seeking harmony at any price within the group – and in the process increasingly loses touch, over the years, with what she herself actually wants.
SX9: Not because she lacks the strength for it, but because the deepest fulfillment for this subtype lies precisely in disappearing into the other: this is how the sexual Nine's system, merging with the partner, never finds its own, independent movement over the decades, even if that means never finding her own direction.
No subtype is immune to atherosclerosis, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes negotiates, in its own way, with the slow, often decades-long process of hardening and narrowing – some through sustained tension and control, others through withdrawal, exhaustion, or a need of their own that was never heard. This is exactly where this Compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outer symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance. When this life force – regardless of which of the 27 subtypes is affected – is brought back into balance, the symptom picture can resolve holistically, instead of merely being suppressed on the surface.

High Blood Pressure (Hypertension) (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When inner pressure is no longer allowed to be expressed and stays in the body instead.
Definition: High blood pressure (arterial hypertension) refers to a persistently elevated pressure of the blood within the arteries – readings of 140/90 mmHg or higher are generally classified as hypertension. In most cases (around 90 percent) this is so-called primary or essential hypertension, where no single physical cause is found, but rather an interplay of predisposition, lifestyle, diet, weight, alcohol, and chronic stress. Left untreated, chronic hypertension significantly raises the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney damage, and atherosclerosis over the years – precisely because it stays unnoticed for so long, medicine calls it the „silent killer“.
Typical symptoms: Usually no noticeable symptoms for years – high blood pressure is often an incidental finding; Occasional morning headaches, especially at the back of the head; Dizziness, ringing in the ears, visual disturbances with markedly elevated readings; Nosebleeds that occur unusually often; Shortness of breath or heart palpitations under exertion; Nervousness, inner restlessness, a diffuse sense of tension that is hard to put into words
Emergency notice: In a hypertensive crisis (blood pressure readings from around 180/120 mmHg) combined with severe headache, visual disturbances, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, or neurological deficits: call emergency services immediately. This can indicate an imminent stroke, heart attack, or organ failure – here every minute counts, this is not the moment for psychosomatic interpretation.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Psychosomatic medicine has long taken the double meaning of pressure literally in cases of hypertension: being „under pressure“, not letting anything show, „swallowing“ one's own anger or exhaustion – phrases that can be found again in the body as measurable physical pressure. Traditional Chinese Medicine assigns many forms of hypertension to rising Liver Yang: an excess and tension energy typically linked to chronically suppressed anger, frustration, or an overabundance of inwardly directed tension. In both views, high blood pressure is less an isolated organ problem than the bodily expression of a system that had to maintain more pressure over a long time than it was ever able to release.
--- Type 1: Anger that never even builds up pressure ---
SE1: Even the slightest flicker of anger is immediately filed and neutralized within the self-preservation One's inner rulebook – nothing may become visible. She is the person who stays calm even at flagrant injustice, while inside a pressure cooker runs at full capacity. Psychosomatic medicine reads exactly this consistent holding back, without ever finding an outlet, as one of the most plausible pictures of a chronically elevated inner pressure that may never discharge – blood pressure as the measurable echo of a control that admits no exceptions.
SO1: Part of the pressure finds an outlet in words and reform-mindedness when the social One turns her anger into moral engagement for the group, yet the underlying tension that the world must be permanently corrected remains. She fights for justice, for better rules, for what is right – and carries the burden that this work is never finished, because somewhere something is always still wrong.
SX1: A disappointing look, an unspoken expectation, and within seconds the tension is palpable – brief, intense, but at least with an outlet the other two variants lack: this is how the sexual One lives out anger more directly, within the relationship itself.
--- Type 2: Pride that asks no one for help ---
SE2: Asking for help feels to the self-preservation Two like admitting weakness – her exhaustion therefore mostly goes unspoken in quiet self-sacrifice. A system that permanently gives more than it receives easily comes under elevated pressure itself: she cares for everyone around her while inwardly under mounting tension herself, without anyone ever noticing – not even herself.
SO2: A chronic overload that can condense over the years into a silent, sustained strain on the entire circulatory system arises from the social Two's inability to say no while she seeks meaning through permanent availability to the community. She always says yes, even when her calendar is already overflowing, because feeling needed matters more than her own well-being.
SX2: Whether she is still enough, whether the beloved might turn away after all: this question drives the inner pressure of the sexual Two, who invests intense, often possessive giving into the one relationship, up in waves that come and subside just as quickly.
--- Type 3: Performance that raises the inner pressure ---
SE3: The inner pressure of constantly having to function is rarely consciously perceived by the self-preservation Three, let alone voiced – she keeps working quietly and efficiently even when her body has long demanded a break. She finishes one task after another without ever asking whether the pace still does her any good.
SO3: A life in competition mode that knows almost no real relaxation phases and comes closest to the classic picture of the Type-A personality is where the social Three seeks success visibly and in constant comparison with others. Every success immediately becomes the new baseline for the next comparison, so real rest is structurally almost never scheduled.
SX3: In every respect the sexual Three wants to be flawless for the one person, deploying permanent self-optimization within the relationship – this demand turns even the most intimate bond into a place where tension never fully lifts.
--- Type 4: Longing that settles in as tension ---

Heart Failure (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When a heart that has given everything for years finally can't anymore.
Definition: Heart failure (cardiac insufficiency) refers to the heart's inability to supply the body with enough blood, and therefore enough oxygen – usually the result of pre-existing damage progressing over years, such as coronary artery disease, chronic high blood pressure, a previous heart attack, or heart valve disease. Unlike an acute heart attack, heart failure is generally not a sudden catastrophe but a gradual process of the heart muscle wearing itself out, often over years. Severity is classified according to the NYHA scale (I to IV), from barely noticeable limitation to symptoms already present at rest.
Typical symptoms: Shortness of breath, at first only under exertion, in advanced stages also at rest or lying down; Rapid exhaustion and reduced capacity for everyday activities; Fluid retention (edema) in the ankles and lower legs, in advanced stages also in the abdomen; Rapid, unintended weight gain from fluid retention within a few days; Nighttime coughing, restlessness while lying down, a need to sleep with the upper body raised; Rapid or irregular heartbeat, pale or bluish lips under greater exertion
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden, severe shortness of breath, especially at rest or lying down, combined with anxiety, frothy or pink-tinged sputum, rapid heartbeat, or bluish lips: call emergency services immediately. This can indicate acute decompensation with pulmonary edema – a life-threatening condition requiring immediate emergency medical care, not a moment for psychosomatic interpretation.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Where a heart attack is the sudden, dramatic event, psychosomatic medicine tends to read heart failure as the slow, often decades-long picture of a strength that gave beyond its limits for too long. Traditional Chinese Medicine describes a related state as Heart Qi deficiency or Heart Yang deficiency – an exhaustion of the vital fire energy that arises not from a single shock but from sustained depletion. In this sense, heart failure is less the picture of a sudden break than that of a heart that gave more, for years, than it ever received back – until its own substance is exhausted.

Atrial Fibrillation (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When the body's own rhythm is lost and chaotic quivering takes its place.
Definition: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained heart rhythm disorder: instead of contracting in an orderly rhythm, the heart's atria contract chaotically and far too fast – up to 350 to 600 times per minute, with no effective pumping action. The ventricles pick up only part of these irregular electrical signals, which shows up as an irregular, often too-fast pulse. Atrial fibrillation can occur in episodes (paroxysmal, with a spontaneous return to normal rhythm), persist for longer periods (persistent), or become permanent. It is promoted by, among other things, high blood pressure, heart valve disease, an overactive thyroid, sleep apnea, alcohol, and advancing age. The greatest danger lies in blood clots forming in the no-longer-effectively-pumping atria, which can trigger a stroke.
Typical symptoms: Fluttering, palpitations, or an irregular, 'flickering' heartbeat; Sometimes completely symptom-free – atrial fibrillation is then discovered incidentally during an examination; Sudden exhaustion, weakness, or reduced exercise capacity; Dizziness, lightheadedness, occasionally shortness of breath; A feeling of tightness or slight pressure in the chest; Inner restlessness or anxiety accompanying the noticeable, irregular heartbeat
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden, very fast and irregular heartbeat combined with severe dizziness, fainting, severe chest pain, or signs of a stroke (e.g. sudden speech, vision, or movement problems): call emergency services immediately. Atrial fibrillation itself is usually not an acute emergency, but it can trigger a stroke or occur alongside another emergency – when in doubt, always seek medical advice.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
The very name carries the psychosomatic interpretation within it: a „flickering“ instead of an orderly beat, a loss of one's own rhythm in favor of chaotic, far too rapid quivering. Traditional Chinese Medicine often assigns irregular heart rhythms to a disturbance of the Heart Shen – the spirit that resides in the heart and is responsible for inner calm, clarity, and orderly thought. When the Shen is thrown off balance by too many simultaneous stimuli, worries, or emotional overload, the heartbeat, too, loses its calm rhythm. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads atrial fibrillation as the picture of a life that has lost its own, reliable rhythm – overstimulated, fragmented, or pulled in too many directions at once.

But if something tips outside her control, if plans get thwarted or mistakes appear she couldn't prevent, this very loss of control can psychosomatically become the picture of a heartbeat losing its orderly rhythm: the outer order was never more than a prop for an inner restlessness that becomes immediately palpable at every disturbance.

The multitude of wrongs she keeps in view and wants to correct simultaneously can settle as too many simultaneous inner stimuli, taking her own heartbeat its calm rhythm.

Coronary Artery Disease / Angina Pectoris (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When the body marks the same invisible limit every time it is pushed.
Definition: Coronary artery disease (CAD) refers to the narrowing of the coronary arteries, caused by atherosclerosis, that supply blood to the heart muscle. When blood flow under exertion is no longer sufficient, angina pectoris results (Latin for „chest tightness“): an episodic, usually pressure-like pain behind the breastbone. In stable angina pectoris, the pain occurs reproducibly at a certain exertion threshold and eases within a few minutes at rest or after taking nitroglycerin. In unstable angina pectoris, the pain is new, worsening, longer-lasting, or already occurring at rest – a medical emergency, since it can directly precede a heart attack.
Typical symptoms: Pressure, tightness, or a burning sensation behind the breastbone, typically under physical or emotional exertion; Pain radiating into the left arm, jaw, neck, back, or upper abdomen; Symptoms easing within a few minutes at rest or after taking nitroglycerin (stable angina pectoris); Shortness of breath or a sense of being winded under exertion; In women, older adults, and diabetics, often less typical: a diffuse feeling of pressure, nausea, or exhaustion instead of classic chest pain; Increasing symptoms at ever lower levels of exertion as a warning sign of worsening disease
Emergency notice: In the case of new, worsening, chest pain lasting longer than 5 minutes, or chest pain already occurring at rest, especially if it does not respond to nitroglycerin: call emergency services immediately. This can indicate unstable angina pectoris or the onset of a heart attack – here every minute counts, this is not the moment for psychosomatic interpretation.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Unlike the one-time, catastrophic heart attack or the decades-long silent progression of atherosclerosis, angina pectoris shows up as a recurring, almost reliable signal: at a certain exertion threshold, the pain announces itself, disappears again at rest – and returns with the next exertion. Traditional Chinese Medicine describes a related state as Xiong Bi, the „painful obstruction syndrome of the chest“: a stagnation of Qi and Blood in the chest that intensifies precisely when more flow is demanded than the system can release. Psychosomatic medicine often reads this recurring pattern as the picture of an always-the-same, invisible limit – a point at which the body reliably objects the moment the demand exceeds a certain measure.

Psychosomatic medicine reads this persistent overriding of her own physical warning signs as a plausible picture of angina pectoris: a pain that reliably objects at a certain exertion threshold, because the person herself would never voluntarily voice that objection.

This permanent, self-imposed overextension in service of a higher cause can show up as a physical limit that keeps announcing itself once moral demand exceeds her own capacity.

Varicose Veins (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When what should flow back instead pools and stagnates.
Definition: Varicose veins refer to enlarged, twisted superficial veins, usually in the legs. The cause is weakened vein valves that normally prevent blood from flowing backward on its way to the heart. When these valves stop working properly, blood pools, the veins widen, and become visible. Development is promoted by genetic predisposition, prolonged standing or sitting, pregnancy, being overweight, and advancing age. Left untreated, chronic venous insufficiency can develop over the years, with skin changes, edema, and, in advanced cases, open leg ulcers (venous ulcers).
Typical symptoms: Visible, twisted, bluish-purple veins, usually on the calves or thighs; A feeling of heaviness, tension, or tiredness in the legs that increases over the course of the day; Evening swelling (edema) at the ankles and lower legs; Nighttime calf cramps; Itching over the affected veins; In advanced disease: brownish skin discoloration, hardening, or open sores on the lower leg
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden, severe swelling, redness, warmth, and pain in one leg (suspected deep vein thrombosis), or sudden shortness of breath and chest pain (suspected pulmonary embolism as a possible complication): seek medical help immediately or call emergency services. Varicose veins themselves are usually not an emergency, but their complications can be.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Unlike arteries, veins are not a driving but a returning structure: they carry blood back to the heart against gravity – a passive return flow that depends on functioning valves and the movement of the leg muscles. Traditional Chinese Medicine assigns the ability to hold tissue, organs, and blood vessels in their place to Spleen Qi – if this is weakened by sustained overload, rumination, or overwork, the body loses its structural firmness, things „sag“ or pool. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads varicose veins not as a picture of excessive pressure, but as one of disturbed letting go: a burden carried for too long, without the return path – the relief, the emptying out again – ever really taking place.
--- Type 1: Duty-load that dams up because letting go feels like negligence ---
SE1: Letting go feels to the self-preservation One like a loss of control she won't allow herself – responsibility and duties are therefore often carried silently for years without ever being consciously released. Psychosomatic medicine reads exactly this pattern of carrying a burden without ever truly handing it off as a plausible picture for varicose veins: a return flow that never happens, because the system is built to hold on to everything.
SO1: Without ever consciously closing old ones, the social One continually takes on new tasks in service of a better community – a mountain of moral responsibility that piles up over the years instead of easing. This ever-growing, never truly discharged burden can show up physically as a backup in the return flow.
SX1: Often with the demand to arrange everything perfectly, the sexual One invests her drive for improvement in a concentrated way into the one relationship – this focused but intense effort produces more isolated tension in individual relationship phases than an evenly accumulated congestion over the years.

A venous system that carries blood in only one direction, its return flow disrupted, reads as one of the most direct pictures of this never-reciprocated cycle of giving.
SO2: Rarely does the social Two accept anything herself while continually placing herself in service of the community – this structural imbalance between giving and receiving can show up physically as a disrupted return flow, in which her own relief never arrives because it simply isn't accounted for.

Thrombosis (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When pooling turns into a solid, immovable block.
Definition: Thrombosis refers to the formation of a blood clot (thrombus) inside a blood vessel that partially or completely blocks blood flow. The deep leg veins are most commonly affected (deep vein thrombosis, DVT). According to Virchow's triad, thrombosis arises from the interplay of three factors: slowed blood flow (stasis, for example from prolonged sitting, lying down, or immobility), damage to the vessel wall, and an increased tendency of the blood to clot (e.g. from hormones, smoking, genetic predisposition, or cancer). The greatest danger is that part of the clot detaches and travels through the bloodstream to the lungs – a pulmonary embolism, which can be life-threatening.
Typical symptoms: Swelling in one leg, often with a feeling of tightness; Pulling, dull pain or a feeling of pressure in the calf or thigh that increases with exertion; Warmth and redness of the affected area of skin; Visibly more pronounced superficial vein pattern; Sometimes only discreet or no symptoms at all, especially with smaller clots; Sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain, or coughing up blood as signs of a possible pulmonary embolism
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain, rapid heartbeat, or coughing up blood: call emergency services immediately – suspected pulmonary embolism. In the case of sudden, marked swelling, pain, warmth, and redness of one leg: seek medical help promptly. A thrombosis should never be self-treated with massage or movement of the affected area – this can dislodge the clot and trigger an emergency.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Where varicose veins show the picture of a pooled but still flowing return, thrombosis goes one step further: pooling turns into a solid, immovable block. The first factor of Virchow's triad – stasis, the slowed or halted flow – already carries this interpretation in the medical term itself. Traditional Chinese Medicine describes a related, further advanced state as Blood stasis (as distinct from mere Blood stagnation): a solidified blockage often linked to long-held, never-released emotional resistance. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads thrombosis as the picture of a life, a decision, or a feeling that has hardened beyond mere stagnation into a fixed, immovable blockage.

SE1: From an initially healthy discipline, a rigid immovability that no longer allows exceptions can develop in the self-preservation One over the years – she holds to once-set rules and procedures even when the situation has long called for adaptation. Psychosomatic medicine reads exactly this hardening, a principle that no longer moves, as a plausible picture of thrombosis: mere congestion becomes a solid, no-longer-dissolvable block.

This progressing rigidity fits the picture of a blockage that has solidified over time.
SX1: In individual, escalated conflicts, the demand for improvement the sexual One brings into the relationship with great intensity can briefly harden into total unyieldingness – with this rigidity here appearing more isolated than solidifying evenly over the years.

Stroke (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When a sudden blow silences what was never allowed to speak.
Definition: A stroke refers to the sudden interruption of blood supply to part of the brain. About 85 percent of cases are ischemic strokes, in which a blood clot blocks a vessel supplying the brain – often as a consequence of atherosclerosis, atrial fibrillation, or an untreated thrombosis. The remaining cases are hemorrhagic strokes, in which a vessel in the brain ruptures and bleeds, usually as a result of untreated high blood pressure. In both cases, brain cells die within minutes if the supply is not quickly restored – a stroke is always a medical emergency, in which every minute determines the extent of lasting damage.
Typical symptoms: Sudden paralysis or numbness, usually on one side of the face, arm, or leg (Face-Arm-Speech test: a drooping corner of the mouth, a sagging arm); Sudden difficulty speaking or understanding speech, slurred or incomprehensible speech; Sudden vision problems in one or both eyes, double vision; Sudden, severe headache with no apparent cause (a warning sign especially of a brain hemorrhage); Sudden dizziness, unsteady gait, or loss of balance; Sudden confusion or clouded consciousness
Emergency notice: For any suspected stroke – even with symptoms that appear only briefly or seem to resolve on their own – call emergency services immediately. Every minute without treatment costs brain tissue: „Time is brain.“ Never wait to see if symptoms improve on their own, and do not drive to the hospital yourself – emergency services can prepare the hospital while already on the way. This section serves purely to interpret an event after it has been survived, never to assess the acute moment.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
The German name already carries the interpretation within it: a „Schlag“ – a blow, a sudden, violent event that strikes exactly where speech, movement, and expression have their origin. Traditional Chinese Medicine often describes stroke as internal wind (Nei Feng): a Liver Yang excess built up over years that suddenly discharges upward and sweeps through the brain like a storm – a direct continuation of the picture already described for high blood pressure. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads stroke as the most dramatic culmination of a pattern already announced in the other conditions of this register: a life, a feeling, or a voice that was never allowed to speak, until the body itself is silenced – sometimes literally, through the loss of speech.
