Low Blood Pressure (Hypotension) (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When a life carries too little pressure to assert itself.
Definition: Hypotension is generally diagnosed at blood pressure readings below about 100–110/60 mmHg. Unlike high blood pressure, low blood pressure is only considered medically treatable if it actually causes symptoms – many people, particularly young, slim women, live symptom-free with permanently low readings. Orthostatic hypotension is common: a drop in blood pressure upon standing up quickly, because the vessels do not adjust fast enough to the change in body position. Causes range from constitutional predisposition, dehydration, and prolonged bed rest to certain medications, hormonal disorders, or a dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system.
Typical symptoms: Dizziness or graying out of vision, especially upon standing quickly; Persistent fatigue, lack of drive, and rapid exhaustion; Cold hands and feet, reduced ability to concentrate; Headaches, ringing in the ears, blurred vision; Heart palpitations as the body's compensatory response to low pressure; In pronounced cases, brief fainting (syncope)
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden fainting with injury, prolonged unconsciousness, chest pain, or signs of circulatory shock (very rapid, barely palpable pulse, pale, cold and clammy skin, confusion): call emergency services immediately. Ordinary, chronic hypotension without such accompanying symptoms is generally not an emergency.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Where most other conditions in this register tell a story of too much pressure – pent-up tension that hardens or suddenly discharges – low blood pressure shows the exact opposite: too little pressure, too little force to assert one's own position outward. Traditional Chinese Medicine describes a related state as Qi deficiency, in particular sinking Middle Qi (Zhong Qi Xia Xian): a lifting force too weak to give the body the energy to carry itself upward and outward. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads this as the picture of a life that rarely asserts itself with full force – not out of suppression, as with the conditions of excess, but out of a fundamental lack of built-up inner drive.
--- Type 1: Anger that never was allowed to show as her own strength ---
SE1: Permanent self-restraint uses up in the self-preservation One exactly the strength that would actually be needed for her own appearance in the world – anger and drive are kept so consistently under control that in the end barely any noticeable energy remains to assert herself outwardly. A system lacking built-up inner pressure, because that pressure was constantly dampened, fits the picture of hypotension.
SO1: Without ever standing up for her own cause, her own position, the social One directs her entire energy toward improving the community – this sustained setting-aside of her own interests in favor of the collective can lead to a chronic lack of self-directed drive.
SX1: Less often does the sexual One lack the strength to assert herself, when she brings her demand into the relationship with direct intensity – exhaustion here shows up more episodically, after especially intense confrontations, than as a chronic lack of baseline energy.
--- Type 2: Giving that never uses her own strength for herself ---
SE2: Simply no strength remains for her own self-assertion, when the self-preservation Two directs every available energy toward others' needs without ever holding anything back for herself. A body permanently lacking the drive to put itself forward reads as a plausible picture of this chronic deficit.
SO2: Only through being needed does the social Two learn early to experience her own significance, as she continually places herself in service of the community – this pattern of never asserting her own worth independent of others can show up as a missing inner drive to give her own cause weight.
SX2: After phases of almost complete investment in the one relationship, a noticeable but rather temporary exhaustion can follow in the sexual Two – more isolated than the other subtypes' chronic, evenly distributed lack of strength.
--- Type 3: Pressure to perform that uses up her own strength for others ---
SE3: Unlike the social Three, the self-preservation Three barely seeks outward recognition – she works quietly and efficiently, often in the background, without visibly asserting her own contribution, which can in the long run mean she lacks the energy to stand up for her own position at all.
SO3: Almost exclusively from outer recognition does the social Three draw her drive – if it fails to appear, or the success goes unnoticed, her inner energy source can genuinely run dry, because she never learned to draw strength from within herself.
SX3: When effort over a longer period doesn't find the hoped-for confirmation: exactly then a lack of strength shows in the sexual Three, who focuses her energy on appearing desirable in the relationship.
--- Type 4: Longing that pulls her own life force inward ---
SE4: The energy it costs to constantly conceal inner suffering can be missing elsewhere for the self-preservation Four, the counter-type: the strength to assert herself emphatically in the world, while she functions outwardly astonishingly composed.
SO4: The social Four draws part of her identity from displayed suffering – this identification with her own pain can paradoxically bind energy that is missing for a forceful everyday self-assertion, because the focus lies more on expressing suffering than on her own drive.
SX4: This intensity itself is a form of strength, even if it doesn't show as a stable, even drive but in fierce waves between upswing and exhaustion: this is how the sexual Four lives uncompromising emotional intensity.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that spares her own energy, but also diminishes it ---
SE5: Deliberately the self-preservation Five reduces her energy consumption, minimizing needs and outer stimuli – this strategy spares scarce resources but can simultaneously mean her body grows accustomed to a permanently low energy level, one that then is also missing where strength is actually needed.
SO5: Even while outwardly taking part in the group, the social Five inwardly withdraws behind her knowledge – this distancing from real emotional engagement can lead to her lacking the energy to advocate for her own position with full force.
SX5: Genuinely lively energy can flow within the narrow bond the sexual Five cultivates – which softens the other Five variants' chronic lack of strength here.
--- Type 6: Fear that binds energy instead of releasing it ---
SE6: Without this energy ever flowing into concrete, powerful action, the self-preservation Six expends much strength mentally rehearsing possible dangers – this circling in advance can mean too little remains in the end for actual self-assertion.
SO6: Instead of using it for her own position, the social Six binds her energy to worry about the collective – this continuous orientation toward outer security rather than inner drive can show up as a lack of self-directed strength.
SX6: Releasing energy in bursts rather than binding it chronically, the sexual Six meets fear counterphobically, through active confrontation – which is why a sustained lack of strength stands less in the foreground here.
--- Type 7: Scattered energy that never really arrives anywhere ---
SE7: Nowhere does enough concentrated strength arrive for real, emphatic self-assertion, even though overall much activity takes place – this is how the self-preservation Seven distributes her energy across many parallel options and projects at once.
SO7: Unlike the unrestrained Seven, the counter-type continually directs her energy toward others' needs, often out of duty – this selfless orientation can lead to a lack of energy reserved for her own cause.
SX7: Rarely does the sexual Seven lack acute energy, living boundless and intense enthusiasm – but the constant search for the next impulse can prevent this strength from ever settling into a stable, lasting self-assertion.
--- Type 8: Strength that flows outward instead of nourishing itself ---
SE8: In the self-preservation Eight, a lack of energy is rare – her strength is usually considerable. If hypotension appears nonetheless, for instance after phases of extreme overextension, it can be read as a rare but clear sign that even this seemingly inexhaustible power source has limits that were consistently exceeded.
SO8: Continually the social Eight puts her strength toward protecting and leading others – if this energy is never balanced by her own regeneration, an exhaustion untypical for this otherwise powerful subtype can creep in over the years.
SX8: If at all, more as a brief dip after especially exhausting emotional escalations does a lack of energy show in the sexual Eight, who lives total intensity in the relationship – not as a chronic baseline state.
--- Type 9: Self-forgetting that builds no strength of its own ---
SE9: In a kind of baseline calm the self-preservation Nine lives, rarely showing her own drive with emphasis – this pattern of never asserting herself with full force, but rather remaining in the comfortable, fits especially precisely the picture of chronically low inner pressure.
SO9: The social Nine forgoes emphasis on her own concerns, continually subordinating her own position to the group – this chronic restraint can show up as a missing drive to stand up for herself.
SX9: Almost exclusively from the bond with the partner does the sexual Nine draw her energy, merging with him – if the partner himself lacks drive or withdraws, this deficit can transfer directly onto her own, never independently built strength.
No subtype is immune to low blood pressure, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is simply that some subtypes – especially those whose core pattern is already oriented toward withdrawal, reserve, or self-forgetting – wrestle especially often with a lack of their own, outward-directed force, while other subtypes, whose pattern relies more on assertion and control, are affected less often. This is exactly where this Compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outer symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance. When this life force – regardless of which of the 27 subtypes is affected – is brought back into balance, the symptom picture can resolve holistically, instead of merely being suppressed on the surface.

Osteoarthritis (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When one's own flexibility wears down over decades instead of being renewed.
Definition: Osteoarthritis refers to the progressive wear of joint cartilage, which normally acts as a cushion between bones, allowing smooth, friction-free movement. As this cartilage wears away, the bones increasingly rub directly against each other, the joint loses mobility, and responds with pain, inflammation, and, in advanced stages, bony outgrowths (osteophytes). The knees, hips, hands, and spine are most commonly affected. Osteoarthritis is promoted by age, being overweight, repeated or uneven strain, previous injuries, and genetic predisposition. Unlike inflammatory rheumatic diseases, osteoarthritis is primarily a mechanical, degenerative process rather than a primarily inflammatory one.
Typical symptoms: Joint pain that typically increases with exertion and eases at rest (in advanced stages, also pain at rest); Morning stiffness of the joints that usually resolves within a few minutes – unlike inflammatory joint disease; Start-up pain: discomfort at the beginning of movement that improves after a short time; Grinding or grating sounds in the joint during movement (crepitus); Increasingly limited mobility of the affected joint; Joint swelling, visible deformity, or increased joint circumference in advanced stages
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden, very severe joint pain with redness, warmth, swelling, and fever: seek medical help promptly – this can indicate acute joint inflammation, a gout attack, or a bacterial joint infection, which differs from ordinary osteoarthritis and should be treated quickly. Ordinary, chronically progressive osteoarthritis is generally not an emergency.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Joints are, within the body, the very sites of mobility – where rigid bones connect in a way that makes movement, changes of direction, and adaptation possible in the first place. Traditional Chinese Medicine assigns bones and joints primarily to the Kidneys (to Jing, the life essence that naturally diminishes with age), while tendons and ligaments belong to the Liver. Kidney weakness combined with poorly nourished tendons is considered there a classic picture of progressive joint complaints. Psychosomatic medicine often reads a related image in osteoarthritis: a rigidity lived over decades – too little adaptability, too much friction from always the same, unchanged movement patterns – that wears down exactly the place that should be responsible for flexibility and change of direction.
--- Type 1: Rigid principles that won't admit wear ---
SE1: Deviation feels wrong, adaptation like negligence: over decades the self-preservation One repeats the same, strictly controlled movement patterns and routines. Psychosomatic medicine reads exactly this ever-identical, never-varied pattern, which allows no flexibility, as a plausible picture of arthritis: a joint that wears down because it never got the chance to move in a new way.
SO1: Often without ever questioning them, the social One holds with great persistence to her moral principles for improving the community – this inner stance, unchanged over the years, can show up as a rigidity reflected physically in joints that likewise show little mobility.
SX1: Changeable between demand and yielding: this dynamic shapes the sexual One as she brings her demand for improvement with intensity into the one relationship – it produces less the even, decades-accumulated friction typical of arthritis than episodic tension.
--- Type 2: Ever-identical giving that allows no new movement ---
SE2: Always being there for others, without ever questioning this role: this is how the self-preservation Two repeats for decades the same pattern of quiet, never-reciprocated giving. This unchanging stance can show up as a kind of physical rigidity, in which her own mobility wears down in favor of the ever-same caretaking posture.
SO2: Without ever questioning it, the social Two continually repeats within the community the same role of tireless availability – this position, unchanged over years, can lead to a rigidity that also shows on a physical level as a lack of adaptability.
SX2: With varying intensity the sexual Two invests herself in shifting, intense relationship phases – this variability stands against the rigid repetition typical of arthritis, even though individual phases themselves can be very demanding.
--- Type 3: An ever-identical path to success that allows no course correction ---
SE3: Because it works, it's never changed: the self-preservation Three holds to a once-proven, efficient work pattern and repeats the same movements over the years. This refusal can produce exactly the one-sided, repeated strain that mechanically wears joints down the most.
SO3: Without varying it, the social Three pursues over the years the same path to success, the ever-identical pattern of performance and recognition – this unchanging orientation can show up as a rigidity that also physically allows for less and less adaptability.
SX3: Strongly to the given relationship and its expectations, the sexual Three adapts her behavior – this adaptability in the relational context can at least partly counteract the rigid repetition typical of arthritis.
--- Type 4: A held-fast longing that permits no new movement ---
SE4: Never expressing what is actually felt: to this ever-identical inner pattern the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, holds unchanged for years. It can show up as a rigidity reflected in a lack of flexibility on the physical level too.
SO4: The social Four holds to no rigid role, showing herself to the group sometimes vulnerable, sometimes combative, depending on what the situation calls for – this flexibility in emotional expression can counteract the rigid, ever-identical repetition especially typical of arthritis.
SX4: From relationship to relationship, from moment to moment, the sexual Four's uncompromising emotional intensity changes strongly – this high emotional variability stands against the rigid, repeated pattern that especially characterizes arthritis psychosomatically.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that hardens into an unchanging routine ---
SE5: Little movement, little variation over decades: this is how the self-preservation Five withdraws into the same minimalist routines, changing little, avoiding new demands. This unchanged way of life over time fits especially precisely the picture of a joint wearing down through ever-identical, never-varied patterns.
SO5: Without supplementing it with new physical or emotional experiences, the social Five repeats over the years the same intellectual territory, the same thought patterns – this one-sided, unchanging orientation can show up as rigidity physically too.
SX5: Movement and change remain intact in at least one place, within the narrow but lively bond the sexual Five cultivates – which counteracts the other Five variants' complete rigidity.
--- Type 6: Caution that repeats the same safety patterns ---
SE6: Without ever questioning them, the self-preservation Six repeats over the years the same precautions and safety rituals – this unchanging, ever-identical preparation for possible dangers can show up as a rigidity that also leaves less and less room for physical mobility.
SO6: Rarely does the social Six change her social position, holding for years to the same loyalties and group structures – this unchanging anchoring can show up as a rigidity that also reflects physically as a lack of adaptability.
SX6: Actively the sexual Six seeks new challenges and confrontations, meeting fear counterphobically – this readiness to keep facing new situations stands against the rigid repetition especially typical of arthritis.
--- Type 7: Apparent variety that repeats the same flight movement ---
SE7: Avoiding the unpleasant, jumping to the next option: this pattern repeats itself at the core over the years, even though the self-preservation Seven appears varied on the outside. This structural repetition beneath the surface of variety can show up as a rigidity that reflects physically too.
SO7: Without varying it, the social Seven, the counter-type, takes on over the years the same selfless, duty-bound role for others – this unchanging position can show up as a rigidity that also allows physically for less and less flexibility.
SX7: Between enthusiasms the sexual Seven switches impulsively, living real, spontaneous variety – this genuine variability stands against the rigid, repeated movement especially typical of arthritis psychosomatically.
--- Type 8: An unyielding stance that allows no adaptation ---
SE8: Rarely does the self-preservation Eight deviate from her course, holding for years to the same forceful, controlled stance – this unyieldingness, which doesn't adapt even when flexibility would be wiser, fits the picture of a mechanical wear accumulated over decades.
SO8: Without varying it, the social Eight takes on over the years the same leadership and protector role – this unchanging position of responsibility can show up as a rigidity that also reflects physically as a lack of adaptability.
SX8: Fierce but shifting: this is how the fluctuations between control and devotion show up, with which the sexual Eight lives total intensity in the relationship – this emotional variability stands against the rigid, ever-identical repetition especially typical of arthritis.
--- Type 9: Inertia that carries the same immobility forward over decades ---
SE9: For decades the self-preservation Nine remains in the same comfortable routine, avoiding any change, any new movement – this sustained persistence in the ever-same is psychosomatically one of the most direct pictures of arthritis: a joint that wears down because it never got the chance to move in a new way.
SO9: Any position change that could cause friction is avoided by the social Nine, who continually subordinates herself over the years to the same role within the group – this chronic immobility can show up as a rigidity that reflects physically too.
SX9: Unchanged over the years, the sexual Nine often takes on the partner's rhythm of life as her own, merging with him – if this merging persists over decades, the missing, independent movement of her own can likewise show up as a form of rigidity.
No subtype is immune to osteoarthritis, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes negotiates mobility, adaptation, and repetition in its own way – some through rigid control, others through lack of movement, overuse, or unchanged routines. This is exactly where this Compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outer symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance. When this life force – regardless of which of the 27 subtypes is affected – is brought back into balance, the symptom picture can resolve holistically, instead of merely being suppressed on the surface.

Back Pain / Herniated Disc (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When the back carries a load that was never meant to be carried alone.
Definition: Back pain is among the most common complaints of all, most often affecting the lumbar spine. A distinction is made between acute (up to 6 weeks), subacute, and chronic back pain (longer than 12 weeks). In most cases, the cause is so-called non-specific – muscular tension, poor posture, lack of movement – without any structural damage being detectable. A herniated disc occurs when the gel-like core of a disc pushes out through the outer fibrous ring and presses on a nerve – often accompanied by pain radiating into the leg (sciatica) or arm. Not every herniated disc causes symptoms; many are discovered incidentally during examinations without ever having triggered any complaints.
Typical symptoms: Pain localized to the back or radiating into the leg or arm, often increasing with movement or certain postures; Muscle tension or palpable hardening of the back muscles; Tingling, numbness, or weakness in the leg or arm when a nerve is involved (radiculopathy); Limited mobility of the spine, difficulty bending or straightening up; Increased pain when coughing, sneezing, or straining, when a disc is involved; Chronic, dull, persistent pain with no clear trigger in longer-standing complaints
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the area of the buttocks or inner thighs („saddle anesthesia“), or rapidly progressing weakness in one or both legs: call emergency services immediately. This can indicate cauda equina syndrome, a rare but acutely surgery-requiring emergency. In the case of new, very severe back pain after a fall or accident, especially in older adults, seek prompt medical evaluation (fracture risk).
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Hardly any part of the body carries as many figures of speech as the back: to „have someone's back“, to „carry a burden on one's back“, to „bend under the weight“, to „show backbone“. Traditional Chinese Medicine assigns the lower back directly to the Kidneys – the „residence of the Kidneys“, as classical texts put it – the very organ system also responsible for willpower (Zhi) and the ability to hold up under pressure. Chronic fear and exhaustion of Kidney energy are considered classic triggers of persistent lower back pain there. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads back pain as a picture that aligns with both views: a burden carried alone and unsupported for too long, a responsibility that should have rested on more shoulders, or a life that rarely got to stand fully upright and show its full stature.
--- Type 1: Duty-load no one may share ---
SE1: Accepting support feels to the self-preservation One like a loss of control – she therefore carries responsibility for the correct running of her own life alone for years, never asking for help. Psychosomatic medicine reads exactly this burden carried alone over decades as a plausible picture for back pain: a back shouldering a responsibility that actually belonged on more shoulders.
SO1: Often without this burden ever being shared, the social One continually takes on the moral responsibility for improving her community – this growing mountain of self-imposed responsibility can show up physically as back pain, right where burdens are carried.
SX1: Often with the feeling of being solely responsible for the relationship's rightness, the sexual One brings her demand into the one relationship with intensity – this focused but isolated burden produces more episodic tension than an evenly accumulated back strain over the years.
--- Type 2: Care that never makes her own burden visible ---
SE2: A back that literally carries everything others need, while her own burden never becomes visible: this is how the self-preservation Two carries others' needs without ever naming her own or asking for relief. That is psychosomatically one of the most direct pictures of this chronically unnoticed pressure.
SO2: Without ever demanding support, the social Two takes on many tasks at once, continually placing herself in service of the community – this invisible, never-shared burden can show up physically as back pain.
SX2: Almost completely the sexual Two invests herself in intense relationship phases – this isolated, highly emotional effort produces more local strain peaks than an evenly distributed everyday back load.
--- Type 3: Pressure to perform that allows no support ---
SE3: Accepting help contradicts the self-image of independent capability – the self-preservation Three keeps working efficiently and alone even when her back has long asked for relief. This consistent carrying alone can show up over the years as chronic back pain.
SO3: Mostly without ever showing it openly, the social Three carries the pressure of constantly holding her own in comparison with others – this invisible burden of permanent performance demand can settle physically as back pain.
SX3: Appearing successful in the relationship: on this the sexual Three concentrates her energy – this focused effort produces more isolated strain peaks in charged relationship moments than a chronic, evenly distributed load.
--- Type 4: Emotional burden that was never allowed to straighten up ---
SE4: A back that literally bends under years of unspoken longing: this is how the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, carries intense inner suffering tenaciously and silently, without ever expressing it. That can psychosomatically be read as one of the most plausible pictures of this never-set-down emotional pressure.
SO4: The social Four speaks openly about the burdens she carries, rather than dragging them along in silence – this outward expression can act as a valve that at least partly counteracts a purely physical back load, even though the underlying longing itself remains.
SX4: Fierce but lived out: this is how the swings between closeness and despair that mark the sexual Four's uncompromising emotional intensity show up – they produce more isolated inner tension than an evenly accumulated back load over the years.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that makes the burden invisible but doesn't dissolve it ---
SE5: Without ever asking for support, the self-preservation Five carries her worries alone and withdraws – this consistent self-isolation, especially regarding emotional burdens, fits the picture of a back carrying a load that was never shared.
SO5: Behind intellectual distance, the social Five hides her own inner burden, keeping herself available to the group with her knowledge – this constant holding-back can show up physically as back pain, where repressed tension settles.
SX5: Genuine relief can take place in at least one place, within the narrow bond the sexual Five cultivates – which counteracts the other Five variants' complete isolation.
--- Type 6: Worry carried as a silent burden ---
SE6: Often without ever openly naming this fear, the self-preservation Six carries constant worry about possible dangers with her – a nervous system in permanent alertness that is never truly relieved fits the picture of a back under unnamed worry.
SO6: Rarely shared is the burden of felt responsibility for her group's well-being that the social Six carries – this collective, never-relieved worry can show up over the years as back pain.
SX6: Outwardly the fear discharges that the sexual Six meets counterphobically through active confrontation – this can prevent the inner burden from accumulating into an evenly built-up back tension.
--- Type 7: A self-imposed burden behind apparent lightness ---
SE7: As soon as the pace slackens, what the self-preservation Seven's permanent scattering – constantly in motion, jumping from option to option – has so far prevented becomes visible: that she ever arrives at her own, deeper exhaustion, which dams up unnoticed and then shows up physically as back pain.
SO7: Often without ever admitting this burden, the social Seven, the counter-type, takes on responsibility for others out of duty – this selfless, never-voiced overextension can show up over the years as chronic back pain.
SX7: Most likely in the rare moments in which she's forced to remain on one commitment does real, accumulated burden show in the sexual Seven, who lives boundless enthusiasm and jumps impulsively from one intensity to the next.
--- Type 8: A protector's burden that allows no weakness ---
SE8: Accepting help fundamentally contradicts the self-preservation Eight's self-understanding – she secures her territory and carries the full responsibility for it alone. This consistent carrying alone of an often considerable burden fits especially precisely the picture of chronic back pain.
SO8: No exhaustion of her own is allowed by the protector role in which the social Eight carries responsibility for many people at once – this permanent, never-shared burden can show up over the years as back pain.
SX8: In charged relationship moments, the extreme but concentrated emotional force with which the sexual Eight lives total intensity produces more isolated strain peaks than an evenly accumulated back load.
--- Type 9: A repressed burden that bends her own back ---
SE9: To avoid her own concerns and conflicts, the self-preservation Nine flees into comfort and routine – this sustained avoidance prevents an inner burden from ever being consciously perceived and thereby relieved, showing up physically as back pain instead.
SO9: Again and again the social Nine gives up her own voice, continually subordinating her own needs to the group's – this chronic self-effacement can show up as a back that never straightens under others' expectations.
SX9: While her own concerns recede, the sexual Nine takes on the partner's as her own, merging with him – this sustained self-abandonment can mean her own burden is never truly recognized as such, because it disappears behind the partner's.
No subtype is immune to back pain or a herniated disc, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes negotiates load, support, and its own backbone in its own way – some through carrying alone and control, others through withdrawal, overload, or a burden of their own that was never set down. This is exactly where this Compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outer symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance. When this life force – regardless of which of the 27 subtypes is affected – is brought back into balance, the symptom picture can resolve holistically, instead of merely being suppressed on the surface.

Rheumatoid Arthritis (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When the body turns against the very joints meant to make movement possible.
Definition: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which the body's own immune system mistakenly attacks the inner lining of the joints (synovial membrane). The resulting chronic inflammation leads to swelling, pain, and, if untreated, the progressive destruction of cartilage and bone. Unlike mechanically caused osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis typically begins symmetrically in small joints – often first in the fingers and wrists – and can spread to numerous other joints and, in severe cases, to internal organs. The exact cause is not conclusively established; a combination of genetic predisposition, environmental factors, and a misdirected immune response is considered likely.
Typical symptoms: Symmetrical swelling and pain in small joints, usually starting in the fingers and wrists; Pronounced morning stiffness typically lasting longer than an hour – unlike osteoarthritis; Warmth and redness over the affected joints; General exhaustion, fatigue, occasionally mild fever; Rheumatoid nodules (palpable lumps under the skin) in advanced disease; Progressively increasing joint deformity and limited mobility if untreated
Emergency notice: Rheumatoid arthritis itself is generally not an acute emergency, but should be evaluated by a rheumatologist at first signs, since early treatment can significantly slow progression. In the case of sudden high fever, severe worsening of the disease, or signs of internal organ involvement (e.g. shortness of breath, chest pain): seek medical help promptly.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
As an autoimmune disease, rheumatoid arthritis occupies a special place among joint conditions: here the body turns not against external strain, but against itself. Psychosomatic medicine often reads this as a picture of inwardly directed harshness – a system that has learned, over the years, to treat itself with the same uncompromising force it actually meant to direct against outside threats. Traditional Chinese Medicine assigns many inflammatory joint complaints to Bi syndrome – a blockage caused by external factors such as Wind, Cold, and Dampness that settles in the joints, often promoted by an already weakened underlying system. In both views, rheumatoid arthritis is less external wear than an inner conflict breaking through into the body.
--- Type 1: Self-criticism that turns against her own body ---
SE1: Never aimed at outer enemies, but at her own inadequacy: this is how the self-preservation One directs her strict inner criticism consistently against herself, checking every impulse of her own for fault. Psychosomatic medicine reads this permanent self-condemnation as one of the most direct pictures of rheumatoid arthritis: an immune system that turns against her own body with the same relentlessness with which the One judges herself.
SO1: Outwardly the social One fights for improving her community, but also continually directs her high moral demand against herself when she feels she hasn't done enough – this inner self-attack can show up physically as a disease in which the system chooses itself as the target.
SX1: More outward, at the beloved and the relationship, does the sexual One direct her criticism than consistently against herself – this externalization can at least partly soften the inward-directed self-attack psychosomatically typical of rheumatoid arthritis.
--- Type 2: Denied neediness that turns against her own body ---
SE2: Her own care never reaches the self-preservation Two's own body – she denies her own needs so consistently that this radical self-overriding can show up as an immune system that literally attacks its own body, because it never learned to treat it as worth protecting.
SO2: Systematically the social Two overrides her own boundaries while continually placing herself in service of the community – this chronic self-denial in favor of others can show up physically as a system that consistently directs its own care outward while attacking itself.
SX2: At least in this one place, a form of emotional exchange and return flow is enabled by the care the sexual Two directs intensely toward the one beloved person – this focused devotion can somewhat soften the complete self-attack possible in other Two variants.
--- Type 3: A demand for performance that tolerates no weakness of her own ---
SE3: Every sign of weakness is judged as personal failure and dealt with just as harshly: this is how the self-preservation Three demands uncompromising performance from herself, even when her body has long signaled exhaustion. This inner harshness against herself fits the picture of an immune system turning against her own body.
SO3: As soon as she falls behind in comparison, the social Three harshly devalues herself, continually measuring herself against others' success – this ongoing inner self-devaluation can settle physically as a system that chooses itself as the target.
SX3: Onto the relationship and the image the beloved holds of her, the sexual Three strongly directs her perfectionism – this outward orientation can at least partly soften the inward-directed self-attack typical of rheumatoid arthritis.
--- Type 4: Self-condemnation arising from unfulfilled longing ---
SE4: Never voiced outward, but directed against herself: this is how the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, holds back her suffering and directs her disappointment over her own perceived inadequacy against herself. This self-condemnation fits especially precisely the picture of an immune system turning against her own body.
SO4: The social Four directs her emotional intensity more outward than consistently against herself, speaking her suffering openly instead of condemning it inwardly – this expression can somewhat soften the complete self-attack possible in other Four variants, even though the underlying longing remains.

Osteoporosis (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When one's own substance diminishes for decades without being noticed for a long time.
Definition: Osteoporosis refers to a chronic disease of the skeleton in which bone density decreases and the inner structure of the bones progressively deteriorates. The bones become more porous, lose stability, and fracture more easily even under minor strain – typically in the vertebrae, femoral neck, or wrist. Women are especially affected after menopause due to estrogen deficiency, but men also develop the disease, particularly at older ages. Other risk factors include lack of movement, calcium and vitamin D deficiency, smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, certain medications (such as cortisone), and genetic predisposition. Osteoporosis itself usually causes no symptoms for years and is often only discovered through a bone fracture – which is why medicine sometimes calls it the „silent disease“.
Typical symptoms: Usually no noticeable symptoms for years – the disease remains unnoticed for a long time; Back pain from changes in the vertebrae, often gradually increasing; Loss of height over the years; Increasing rounding of the upper back („dowager's hump“) in advanced stages; Bone fractures from minor falls or strains, often the first visible sign of the disease; Persistent back pain after a seemingly harmless fall can indicate a vertebral fracture
Emergency notice: Osteoporosis itself is not an acute emergency. In the case of sudden, severe back pain after a fall or strain, especially combined with a known osteoporosis diagnosis or at an older age, and with any suspected bone fracture (e.g. after a fall onto the hip or wrist): seek medical help promptly.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Bones are the innermost scaffolding of the body – the structure that gives everything else its support, usually invisible and given little attention until it gives way. Traditional Chinese Medicine assigns bone substance directly to the Kidneys and to Jing, the life essence that naturally diminishes with age, but can also be used up faster through chronic exhaustion, insufficient self-care, or a life lived without adequate inner reserves. Psychosomatic medicine often reads a picture in osteoporosis that shares exactly this invisibility: a substance that diminishes unseen over decades because it never received enough attention, nourishment, or care, until the deficiency suddenly and unmistakably shows itself.

Fibromyalgia (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When the whole body reports pain without a single place where anything can be found.
Definition: Fibromyalgia (fibromyalgia syndrome) is a chronic pain condition characterized by widespread, often shifting pain in muscles, tendons, and joints, usually accompanied by pronounced exhaustion, sleep disturbances, and cognitive impairment („fibro fog“). Unlike inflammatory or degenerative joint diseases, laboratory and imaging tests show no structural abnormalities – diagnosis rests on the characteristic symptom picture and the exclusion of other causes. The exact origin remains incompletely understood to this day; a disturbed pain processing in the central nervous system is discussed, often in interplay with chronic stress, earlier traumatic experiences, and heightened pain sensitivity.
Typical symptoms: Chronic, widespread pain in muscles and connective tissue, often shifting to different parts of the body; Pronounced exhaustion that barely improves even with sleep; Unrefreshing sleep despite adequate sleep duration; Difficulties with concentration and memory („fibro fog“); Increased tenderness at certain points of the body (tender points); Frequently accompanying complaints such as irritable bowel, headaches, sensitivity to cold or heat, inner restlessness
Emergency notice: Fibromyalgia itself is not an acute emergency. However, since the symptoms can resemble other, sometimes more serious conditions, newly appearing or strongly changing symptoms should be medically evaluated to rule out other causes (such as inflammatory rheumatic or neurological diseases).
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Among the conditions of the musculoskeletal system, fibromyalgia occupies a special place: the pain is real and often considerable, yet it cannot be pinned to any single structure – as if not one joint or tendon were affected, but the entire way the body processes stimuli and strain in the first place. Traditional Chinese Medicine often describes a related state as a combination of Liver Qi stagnation (blocked, non-flowing life energy, frequently from suppressed emotions) and a general exhaustion of Qi and Blood. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads fibromyalgia less as the picture of a local injury than of a system that had to process more, over the years, than it could handle – until the entire body became a resonance chamber for an overload that cannot be pinned down anywhere concrete.

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When exactly the nerve that makes grasping and holding possible gets constricted.
Definition: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve at the wrist, where it runs together with several tendons through a narrow, ligament-enclosed passage – the carpal tunnel. If the tissue in this passage swells, for instance from repetitive strain, inflammatory processes, hormonal changes (often during pregnancy), or anatomical narrowness, the nerve comes under pressure. The result is sensory disturbance and pain in the fingers supplied by the nerve – usually the thumb, index, middle, and part of the ring finger. Left untreated, this can lead to permanent nerve damage with loss of hand strength.
Typical symptoms: Tingling or numbness in the thumb, index, middle, and part of the ring finger, often occurring at night; Wrist pain that can radiate into the forearm; A sense of swollen, clumsy fingers even though no swelling is visible from the outside; Temporary relief from shaking out the hand („flick sign“); Declining fine motor skills, difficulty buttoning clothes or grasping small objects; In advanced stages, noticeable loss of strength and wasting of the thumb muscle
Emergency notice: Carpal tunnel syndrome itself is not an acute emergency, but persistent or worsening symptoms should be medically evaluated to avoid permanent nerve damage. In the case of sudden, complete loss of sensation or pronounced weakness in the hand following an injury: seek medical help promptly.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
The hand is one of the most important tools for the ability to act at all – with it we grasp, hold on, work, give, and receive. When precisely the nerve controlling this ability gets constricted, a psychosomatic reading suggests itself: a situation in which one's own grasping or holding on – whether to a task, a relationship, or a phase of life – is demanded beyond one's own capacity, until exactly the channel through which capability to act flows starts to feel too narrow. Traditional Chinese Medicine often assigns complaints of this kind to local Qi and Blood stagnation, frequently promoted by repeated, monotonous movement without adequate recovery – a picture that aligns with the Western interpretation of an overloaded channel under sustained pressure.

Psychosomatic medicine reads exactly this excessive, never-relenting grasping as a plausible picture of carpal tunnel syndrome: a channel that feels too narrow because grasping never gets a break.

Gout (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When what has accumulated suddenly, sharply, and unmistakably discharges in one joint.
Definition: Gout is a metabolic disease in which elevated uric acid levels in the blood (hyperuricemia) cause uric acid crystals to deposit in the joints. These crystals trigger a sudden, very painful inflammatory reaction – the acute gout attack – which classically affects the big toe joint (podagra) but can also affect other joints. Gout is promoted by genetic predisposition, a purine-rich diet (red meat, offal, certain seafood), excessive alcohol consumption – especially beer –, being overweight, and certain conditions such as high blood pressure or impaired kidney function. Left untreated, recurring gout attacks can lead to chronic joint damage and visible uric acid deposits (tophi).
Typical symptoms: Sudden, very severe pain in a joint, often starting at night or in the early morning hours; Pronounced redness, swelling, and warmth of the affected joint; Extreme sensitivity to touch – even a blanket can feel painful; Classically the big toe joint is affected, but the knee, ankle, fingers, or elbow are also possible; Fever and general malaise during an acute attack; In chronic gout: palpable lumps (tophi) under the skin, especially on the ears, fingers, or elbows
Emergency notice: An acute gout attack is usually not a life-threatening emergency, but should be treated promptly to contain the inflammation. In the case of high fever, pronounced malaise, or uncertainty about whether it is gout or a bacterial joint infection (which requires emergency treatment): seek medical help promptly.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Gout already carries a psychosomatically telling picture in its very development: over weeks, months, or years, something quietly accumulates – excess uric acid – causing no symptoms at first, until it discharges sharply in a single, highly dramatic moment. Historically, gout was often linked to an excessive, indulgent lifestyle – the „disease of kings“, as it was sometimes called. Traditional Chinese Medicine often assigns gout to a combination of Damp-Heat (Shi Re) that pools in the joints, frequently promoted by excessive consumption of rich, heavy, or alcoholic food. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads this as a picture of held-back, accumulated intensity that eventually can no longer be controlled and breaks out explosively at the most sensitive point.

Tennis Elbow (Epicondylitis) (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When the same tensed hand motion is repeated so often that the very point of origin starts to hurt.
Definition: Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) refers to a painful irritation of the tendon insertions at the outer elbow bone, where the forearm's extensor muscles attach. Despite the name, the condition rarely actually arises from playing tennis – far more common are repeated, one-sided strains on the hand and forearm muscles in everyday life or work, such as screen work with a mouse and keyboard, manual trades, or repetitive gripping motions. The constant overload creates tiny micro-injuries in the tendon fibers, which can become chronically inflamed when the tissue is not given adequate recovery. The counterpart at the inner elbow bone is called golfer's elbow.
Typical symptoms: Pain at the outer elbow, typically increasing with exertion (e.g. gripping, lifting, or turning the forearm); Tenderness directly over the bony tendon insertion at the elbow; Painful gripping, e.g. shaking hands, lifting a cup, or opening a bottle cap; Pain radiating into the forearm, sometimes as far as the hand; Increasing weakness when gripping; In chronic cases: persistent discomfort even with minor strain or at rest
Emergency notice: Tennis elbow is not an acute emergency. In the case of sudden, very severe pain after an acute injury, visible swelling, deformity, or inability to move the arm: seek medical help promptly to rule out a fracture or tendon rupture.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Tennis elbow does not arise from a single, dramatic injury, but from the quiet repetition of the same tensed movement, over and over, until exactly the point where strength and movement originate – the tendon insertion – itself becomes the site of pain. Traditional Chinese Medicine often assigns complaints of this kind to a local stagnation of Qi and Blood, usually from repeated, monotonous tension without adequate balance. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads this as a picture of always the same, cramped effort – a task, a role, or a stance carried out again and again with a tensed grip, until exactly the point where this effort begins becomes exhausted.

Psychosomatic medicine reads exactly this ever-same, never-varied tension as a plausible picture of tennis elbow: a point of origin for strength that's exhausted because it never got to learn another, more relaxed movement.

Frozen Shoulder / Shoulder Impingement (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When the shoulder stiffens piece by piece until movement itself becomes barely possible.
Definition: Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) refers to a painful, progressive stiffening of the shoulder joint caused by inflammation and scarring shrinkage of the joint capsule. It typically progresses through three phases: a painful phase with increasing restriction of movement, a „frozen“ phase with pronounced stiffness as pain eases, and a thawing phase in which mobility slowly returns, often over months to years. Shoulder impingement, on the other hand, arises from a narrowing of the space between the upper arm bone and the shoulder blade, often caused by overuse, poor posture, or age-related wear of the rotator cuff tendons. Both conditions affect the same joint and can transition into one another or reinforce each other.
Typical symptoms: Increasing, often gradually beginning shoulder pain that intensifies with movement; Progressive restriction of mobility, especially when lifting the arm overhead or backward; Nighttime pain that makes lying on the affected side difficult; A painful pinching sensation when lifting the arm sideways (typical of impingement); Everyday movements like putting on a jacket or combing hair become increasingly difficult; With frozen shoulder: a phase in which mobility is barely present despite easing pain
Emergency notice: Neither frozen shoulder nor shoulder impingement are acute emergencies. In the case of sudden, very severe shoulder pain after a fall or accident, visible deformity, or complete inability to move the arm: seek medical help promptly to rule out a fracture or shoulder dislocation.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body – it makes embracing possible just as much as rejecting, carrying just as much as letting go, reaching out just as much as withdrawing. Precisely this joint, actually built for maximum mobility, stiffens step by step with frozen shoulder, until movement becomes barely possible. Traditional Chinese Medicine aptly calls this condition „fifty-year-old shoulder“ and assigns it to a combination of Qi and Blood deficiency in older age, often intensified by the invasion of Wind and Cold into an already weakened system. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads this as a picture of increasing rigidity exactly at the place that should actually be responsible for openness, embrace, and allowing closeness – a freedom of movement that restricts itself over time, until it, often just as slowly, releases again.

Sciatica (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When a single, sudden moment locks up the entire back for days.
Definition: Sciatica refers to pain along the sciatic nerve, usually triggered by irritation or compression of the nerve root in the lower back – often caused by a herniated disc, a narrowing of the spinal canal, or muscular tension. The pain typically radiates from the lower back through the buttock into the thigh and calf. Lumbago, by contrast, refers to a suddenly shooting, often severe pain in the lower back itself, usually triggered by an awkward, jerky movement – for instance while bending or straightening up – without a nerve root necessarily being involved. Both conditions often occur together and share the region from which they arise.
Typical symptoms: Suddenly shooting, often lightning-like pain in the lower back (lumbago); Radiating, often burning or pulling pain from the buttock down the back of the leg (sciatica); Worsening of symptoms when coughing, sneezing, or straining; Tense, barely mobile back muscles, often with a pain-driven protective posture; Tingling or numbness in the affected leg when a nerve is involved; Limited ability to bend, straighten up, or turn
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the area of the buttocks or inner thighs („saddle anesthesia“), or rapidly progressing weakness in one or both legs: call emergency services immediately. This can indicate cauda equina syndrome, a rare but acutely surgery-requiring emergency. Ordinary lumbago or sciatica without these warning signs is generally not an emergency, but should be medically evaluated if symptoms persist.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Unlike gradually developing back pain that builds up over years, lumbago and acute sciatica are often a single, sudden moment: one movement too many, a final drop that overflows an already overloaded barrel. Traditional Chinese Medicine often assigns these complaints to a sudden blockage of Qi and Blood in the lower back, frequently triggered by the meeting of an already existing weakness with an acute outer stimulus such as cold or an awkward movement. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads this sudden, lightning-like shooting pain as a picture of those moments when a long-held-back overload can no longer be controlled – not as slow wear, but as a single, unmistakable moment of collapse.

Exactly this moment, in which long-held-back tension can no longer be controlled, psychosomatic medicine reads as a plausible picture of lumbago.

Tendinitis (Psychosomatics Register · Musculoskeletal System)
When the same movement is repeated so often that even the sheath protecting it becomes inflamed.
Definition: Tendinitis of the sheath (tenosynovitis) refers to a painful irritation of the protective gliding sheath that surrounds many tendons and allows them to slide with little friction along the bone. The tendons of the wrist and hand are most commonly affected, less often the foot. The usual cause is repeated, monotonous overload – for instance from typing, playing an instrument, manual trades, or repetitive athletic movements – through which the gliding sheath becomes inflamed and swells, making movement of the tendon increasingly painful and restricted. A particular form is stenosing tenosynovitis (trigger finger), in which the tendon can barely move through the narrowed sheath and snaps abruptly when straightening or bending.
Typical symptoms: Pain along the affected tendon, clearly increasing with movement; Swelling and tenderness over the tendon sheath; A grinding or grating sensation when moving the affected joint (crepitus); With stenosing tenosynovitis: an abrupt, snapping motion of the finger when straightening; Increasing weakness and restricted movement in the affected area; Increased pain with continued, unchanged strain without a break
Emergency notice: Tendinitis is not an acute emergency. In the case of pronounced redness, warmth, fever, or rapidly increasing swelling: seek medical help promptly to rule out a bacterial infection of the tendon sheath, which requires urgent treatment.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
The tendon sheath is a protective covering – it ensures that movement can happen smoothly, without resistance. When it becomes inflamed, precisely what was supposed to make movement easier itself becomes the source of pain. Traditional Chinese Medicine often assigns complaints of this kind to a local stagnation of Qi and Blood, arising from repeated, always-the-same tension without adequate balance – a picture close to tennis elbow, but even more directly located in the protective sheath itself. Psychosomatic medicine therefore often reads this as a picture of excessive friction: a movement, a task, or a role repeated so often and so uniformly that even the protective frame meant to make it possible becomes inflamed.

Psychosomatic medicine reads this monotonous, never-interrupted tension as a plausible picture of tendinitis: a protective sheath that inflames because the movement it was meant to ease never got a break.

Asthma (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
When breathing can no longer be taken freely, but has to be fought for.
Definition: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways in which the bronchi react hypersensitively to a wide range of triggers – allergens, cold air, exertion, infections, or stress. During an acute attack the bronchi narrow through a combination of muscle spasm, swelling of the mucous membrane, and increased mucus production, which makes exhaling in particular much harder. A distinction is made between allergic (extrinsic) asthma, which usually begins in childhood and occurs alongside other atopic conditions such as eczema or hay fever, and non-allergic (intrinsic) asthma, which often first appears in adulthood. Between attacks, those affected can be symptom-free for long stretches – yet the underlying inflammatory readiness of the airways persists.
Typical symptoms: Attacks of shortness of breath, usually with labored, prolonged exhalation; Wheezing or whistling breath sounds, often audible from a distance; Tightness or pressure in the chest; Dry, often nocturnal cough, sometimes the only symptom (cough-variant asthma); Worsening of symptoms with cold, exertion, allergens, infections, or strong smells; Anxiety and restlessness during an acute attack, often accompanied by an upright, forward-leaning posture
Emergency notice: In case of severe shortness of breath that does not improve despite emergency medication, bluish lips, inability to speak full sentences, or rapidly increasing exhaustion: call emergency services immediately. A severe asthma attack (status asthmaticus) is a life-threatening emergency – every minute counts here, and there is no room for psychosomatic interpretation.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Hardly any bodily function is as directly bound to life itself as breathing – and hardly any symptom wears its psychosomatic reading as openly as the labored exhalation of asthma: air is still taken in, but letting go becomes difficult. Traditional Chinese Medicine assigns the lung to the Metal element and to grief – an organ that regulates not only oxygen but also connection to the world and separation from it, in constant exchange between outer and inner. When this exchange falls out of balance, for instance through withheld grief or chronically suppressed feelings, TCM holds that this can show up as tightness of breath. Psychosomatic medicine often reads asthma as an image of spaces, relationships, or expectations that have become so narrow that one's own breath – literally and figuratively – is no longer allowed to flow freely.
--- Type 1: Anger that holds its own breath ---
SE1: The self-preservation One keeps not only her anger but her very breath under disciplined control – deep, free breathing feels to her almost like a loss of control she does not permit herself. Psychosomatic medicine reads this unconscious withholding of one's own breath, bound up with the constant inner tension of keeping her surroundings and herself correct, as an apt image for the tightness of asthma: a lung that is never allowed to fully open, because openness is experienced as a risk.
SO1: The social One fights for the right order of things with palpable inner tension, often never granting herself a genuine breather – this struggle without recovery can show up as breathing that rarely truly settles, but instead remains in a constant, tense state of readiness.
SX1: The sexual One brings her demand for improvement into the one relationship with great intensity – precisely in moments of escalation, when criticism and disappointment collide, this tension can show up as sudden, episodic breathlessness rather than as chronic, ongoing strain.

This self-diminishment, lived out over years, can show up psychosomatically in a lung that is equally reluctant to fully expand and claim its own share of the air.

COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease) (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
When decades of exhaling against resistance rebuild the lung piece by piece.
Definition: COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease) refers to a chronic, progressive narrowing of the airways, usually based on a combination of chronic bronchitis and a breakdown of lung tissue (emphysema). Unlike asthma, the narrowing in COPD is only partially reversible or not reversible at all – the lung itself changes structurally. In Western industrialized nations, the main cause in the vast majority of cases is long-term smoking, less often occupational exposure to pollutants or a genetic alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. COPD usually develops insidiously over decades, is often diagnosed only late, and progresses continuously without consistent treatment – above all, quitting smoking.
Typical symptoms: Chronic cough, often worse in the morning, with or without sputum („smoker's cough“); Increasing shortness of breath, at first only on exertion, in advanced stages also at rest; Wheezing or whistling breath sounds, prolonged exhalation; Reduced physical stamina that develops gradually over years; Frequent respiratory infections that resolve more slowly than in healthy people; In advanced stages: weight loss, bluish lips, barrel chest from an overinflated lung
Emergency notice: In case of suddenly, sharply worsening shortness of breath, bluish lips, confusion, or severe exhaustion: call emergency services immediately. An acute COPD exacerbation can be life-threatening – every minute counts here, and there is no room for psychosomatic interpretation.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Where asthma shows itself in attacks and often resolves again between episodes, COPD is the picture of a condition that has slowly and permanently changed over decades – the lung itself rebuilds, adapting to a permanently limited state. Traditional Chinese Medicine often describes a related condition as chronic Lung Qi deficiency, intensified by the repeated intrusion of outer irritants (smoke, cold) into an already weakened system. Psychosomatic medicine often reads COPD as the picture of a life that has breathed against an inner resistance for a very long time without that resistance ever being changed – until the body has adapted so thoroughly to the restriction that it becomes a permanent condition.
