Chronic Bronchitis (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
When constant coughing becomes the only permitted way of making room for air.
Definition: Chronic bronchitis is diagnosed when a productive cough with sputum is present on most days for at least three months in two consecutive years. The cause is persistent irritation of the bronchial mucous membrane, in the vast majority of cases through cigarette smoke, less often through air pollutants or repeated respiratory infections. The mucous membrane responds with increased mucus production and chronic inflammation, which can narrow the airways over the long term. Chronic bronchitis is considered a precursor to or component of COPD, but it can also persist independently for years without a relevant impairment of lung function yet being present.
Typical symptoms: Persistent cough with sputum, on most days over months; Cough worse in the morning, often right after getting up; Thick, whitish to yellowish-green sputum, worse during infections; Mild to moderate shortness of breath on exertion; Recurring respiratory infections that resolve more slowly than in healthy people; Occasional wheezing breath sound, especially with additional narrowing of the bronchi
Emergency notice: Chronic bronchitis itself is not an acute emergency. In case of suddenly, sharply worsening shortness of breath, high fever, bloody sputum, or severe exhaustion: seek medical help promptly to rule out pneumonia or an acute worsening.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
The cough of chronic bronchitis has something oddly persistent about it: it does not arrive as a single event but as a faithful companion that reports back day after day, often precisely when the body has only just settled. Traditional Chinese Medicine often attributes excessive mucus production to a weakness of the Spleen and Lung – the Spleen is considered the „source of phlegm“, the Lung the organ that „stores“ it and must ultimately release it again. Psychosomatic medicine often reads constant coughing as the picture of a repeated attempt to make room for air and expression – a recurring, almost ritual clearing of the throat that steps in where a more direct way of making oneself heard is apparently unavailable.
--- Type 1: Anger that breaks through in constant coughing ---
SE1: The self-preservation One consistently holds back anger and criticism, never releasing them in words – instead, a different, physical channel opens up: a dry, ever-recurring throat-clearing or cough that arises exactly when inner tension is otherwise not allowed to discharge. Psychosomatic medicine reads this substitute valve as an apt image for chronic bronchitis.
SO1: When the social One cannot or will not voice her moral outrage over injustice directly, this withheld energy can show up as a constant, almost reflexive cough – a physical comment that steps in where words are missing or suppressed.
SX1: Since the sexual One expresses her anger more directly in words within the relationship, this substitute physical valve appears less often – the tension tends to discharge immediately rather than through a constant, chronic cough.
--- Type 2: A swallowed need that shows up as coughing ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two literally swallows her own needs and disappointments, never voicing them – this constant swallowing can show up physically as an irritation in the throat and bronchi that keeps breaking through as coughing, because what actually needs to be said never finds its way out.
SO2: The social Two rarely displays her disappointment over a lack of recognition openly – this constant swallowing of genuine feelings can show up as a chronic irritant cough that reports in exactly where an open conversation should have taken place.
SX2: In intense relationship phases, the sexual Two does express her needs more directly – this more immediate expression counters the constant, substitute coughing more typical of more thoroughly swallowed feelings.
--- Type 3: Achievement that leaves no time for a clarifying expression ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three keeps functioning efficiently even when irritation or exhaustion is already palpable – a brief cough here and there goes barely noticed, let alone taken seriously as a signal. This casual overriding of a constantly recurring cough fits the picture of chronic bronchitis that was able to develop over years unnoticed.
SO3: In constant comparison with others, the social Three has little room left to truly attend to a recurring cough – this overriding of physical signals in favor of outward achievement can, over the long term, show up as chronic irritation of the airways.
SX3: To appear flawless in the relationship, the sexual Three would rather suppress or mask a disruptive cough – this desire for control over her outward image tends to counteract the open, constant coughing seen in other Three variants.
--- Type 4: Longing that shows up as a lingering irritation ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four, the counter-type, carries intense inner suffering stubbornly and silently, without ever expressing it – this sustained withholding can show up physically as a lingering irritation in the airways that reports in as coughing where words are missing.
SO4: The social Four makes her suffering visible and finds a verbal expression in it – this outward expression can act as a valve that at least partly counteracts the purely physical coughing, even though the underlying longing itself remains.
SX4: With fierce but openly lived swings between closeness and despair, the sexual Four's emotional intensity tends to discharge directly within the relationship rather than through a substitute, chronic cough.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that keeps its own irritation to itself ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five consistently keeps even physical complaints to herself, rarely seeking medical advice as long as it is at all possible – this quiet enduring of a lingering cough, without ever seriously treating it, fits the picture of chronic bronchitis that was able to settle in over years untreated.
SO5: The social Five keeps emotional closeness at a distance behind intellectual detachment – a recurring cough, too, can thus be registered as an abstract fact rather than taken seriously as a genuine physical signal.
SX5: Within the narrow, deep bond that the sexual Five cultivates, physical complaints can well be discussed openly – which counteracts the quiet suppression seen in other Five variants.
--- Type 6: Fear that shows up as a nervous cough ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six lives in constant caution and inner tension – this permanent state can show up physically as a nervous, ever-recurring throat-clearing or cough that reports in especially in moments of heightened tension.
SO6: The social Six carries an often unspoken worry for the well-being of her group – this diffuse tension, never fully relieved, can show up as a chronic irritation of the airways.
SX6: Through active confrontation, the sexual Six discharges fear more directly rather than processing it through a substitute cough – this more immediate reaction counters the chronic, nervous cough seen in other Six variants.
--- Type 7: Indulgences that irritate the airways directly ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven secures herself through options and indulgences, often paired with smoking as a means of self-soothing – psychosomatic medicine reads this direct reach for irritants as one of the most immediate pictures of chronic bronchitis: a mucous membrane that has grown accustomed to repeated outer irritation.
SO7: The social Seven, the counter-type, sets her own needs aside in favor of others, often to the point of her own exhaustion – a recurring cough can easily be overlooked in the process, because attention consistently lies with the needs of others.
SX7: The sexual Seven lives out enthusiasm boundlessly, often paired with intense indulgence in stimulants – psychosomatic medicine reads this impulsive intensity as one of the more direct paths to an irritated, chronically inflamed bronchial mucous membrane.
--- Type 8: Control that dismisses coughing as weakness ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight consistently overrides physical warning signs, because admitting weakness contradicts her self-image – a lingering cough is simply ignored until it has settled in as a chronic pattern.
SO8: The social Eight takes on responsibility for many people at once and often puts her own health last in the process – a recurring cough remains unattended until it has structurally settled in.
SX8: In extreme but episodic swings, the sexual Eight lives her intensity within the relationship – this pointed dynamic differs from the chronic, structural coughing pattern more typical of permanently overridden warning signs.
--- Type 9: Self-forgetting that overrides its own cough ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine takes refuge in comfort and routine and often barely consciously registers her own cough – this overlooking of a constantly recurring physical signal fits especially closely with the picture of chronic bronchitis that was able to develop over years unnoticed.
SO9: The social Nine subordinates her own voice so consistently to group harmony that even her own cough rarely finds real attention – this chronic self-effacement can show up as a signal that is never taken seriously yet keeps recurring.
SX9: The sexual Nine merges with her partner and often adopts his or her perception of her own health as the standard – if the partner does not notice the cough, the Nine often does not notice it either, because her own bodily awareness recedes behind the merging.
No subtype is immune to chronic bronchitis, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes negotiates withheld expression, overridden signals, and its own voice in its own way – some through swallowed anger, others through withdrawal, substance-linked self-soothing, or a warning of their own that is never taken seriously. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not with the outward symptom, but with the vital force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance. If this vital force – regardless of which of the 27 subtypes is affected – is brought back into balance, the symptoms can resolve holistically instead of merely being suppressed on the surface.

Hay Fever (Allergic Rhinitis) (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
An overshooting defense reaction of the nasal mucous membrane to essentially harmless substances such as pollen, house dust, or pet hair.
Definition: Hay fever (allergic rhinitis) arises when the immune system mistakes harmless environmental substances – pollen, dust mites, pet hair, mold spores – for a threat and responds with an IgE-mediated immediate reaction. Mast cells in the nasal mucous membrane release histamine, which dilates blood vessels, causes the mucous membrane to swell, and triggers a runny nose, sneezing, a blocked nose, and itchy, watering eyes. A distinction is made between the seasonal form (tied to particular pollen seasons) and the year-round form (e.g. caused by dust mites or pet hair). Left untreated, the irritation can spread to the bronchi over the years – the so-called „allergic march“ from the nose to allergic asthma.
Typical symptoms: Bouts of sneezing, often in volleys; Watery, clear runny nose; Blocked, swollen nasal mucous membrane; Itchy, red, watering eyes; Itching in the nose, palate, or throat; Fatigue and difficulty concentrating during the season
Emergency notice: In case of additional shortness of breath, wheezing breath, or tightness in the chest (a sign of emerging allergic asthma), seek prompt medical evaluation. In case of circulatory symptoms as part of a cross-reactive allergy (e.g. after certain foods), seek medical help immediately.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
In TCM, the nose is considered the opener of the lung, and the lung in turn carries the „Wei Qi“, the defensive energy that protects the body at its outermost boundary against what intrudes from outside. Hay fever can be read as a Wei Qi that has lost its fine calibration: it sounds the alarm over things that pose no real danger at all – pollen, house dust, a single cat hair. Psychosomatically, this corresponds to a sense of boundary that is either too sensitive or too blurred: whoever reacts chronically over-irritated to their environment has an immune system that learns to stay permanently on guard, even where no danger lurks. For each of the 27 subtypes, its own pattern shows how easily its own boundary slips into a state of alarm.
--- Type 1: Anger that keeps strict watch over its own boundary ---
SE1: Cleanliness is a central concern for the self-preservation One, and precisely that can turn against her: where others simply enjoy a spring day, she registers every speck of dust, every cloud of pollen as a disruption of the order she so laboriously maintains. The nasal mucous membrane takes over what the mind has long since learned – to distinguish uncompromisingly between clean and unclean – and sounds the alarm at every deviation.
SO1: The social One considers herself the authority on how things ought to be done properly, and tolerates little that steps out of line – not even at the cellular level. Pollen drifting through an open window is, to her, a small trespass against an order that should really have been observed. The overshooting defense reaction mirrors her low tolerance for the uncontrolled.
SX1: In the sexual One, a demand for perfection combines with intensity – even anger at an environment experienced as imperfect is not managed here but fully lived through. The watering, reddened eyes of hay fever season are almost a visible echo of an inner outrage that the world will not conform to her own high standards.
--- Type 2: Pride that opens its own boundary for others ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two tirelessly looks after others and, in the process, easily forgets to look after her own boundaries. The body takes over what the mind blanks out, responding to every intruding stimulus with immediate alarm – a kind of substitute defense for the boundaries that are given up in everyday life for the sake of others.
SO2: Whoever wants to be socially indispensable finds it hard to say „no, that doesn't agree with me“ – not even to her own nasal mucous membrane. The social Two places herself in service of her surroundings and, in doing so, overlooks that constant openness to everyone and everything also means letting in, unfiltered, whatever is in the air.
SX2: The sexual Two seeks closeness with full intensity and deliberately lets the boundary between herself and her beloved blur. This permeability has its price: pollen and allergens, too, find easier entry when one's own defenses are chronically oriented toward merging rather than boundary-setting.
--- Type 3: Achievement that plays down its own reaction ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three prefers to function smoothly and has little patience for a watering, runny nose during pollen season – it disrupts the image of capability she labors to maintain. Precisely this resistance to any „sign of weakness“ often prevents her from addressing it early, so the reaction grows worse season after season.
SO3: Sneezing in front of others and standing there with red eyes contradicts the image the social Three wants to project, so the allergy is often played down or hastily masked with antihistamines instead of being given the space it needs. The symptom remains an unloved blind spot in an otherwise flawlessly staged performance.
SX3: The sexual Three wants to appear irresistible even under strain, and an itchy, swollen nose does not fit that image. The effort of playing down or ignoring the allergic reaction costs extra energy – energy that is actually needed for recovery and genuine regulation of the over-irritated mucous membrane.
--- Type 4: Longing that underscores its own sensitivity ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four often experiences physical discomfort as further proof that she is more sensitive than others – and indeed, this subtype does tend to perceive environmental stimuli more intensely. The overshooting reaction of the nasal mucous membrane fits into a self-image in which her own experience is fundamentally stronger, finer, more vulnerable than that of others.
SO4: For the social Four, hay fever can become a quiet expression of being different – a suffering that sets her apart from the seemingly carefree majority who simply enjoy spring while she struggles. The symptoms thus unconsciously become part of an identity defined by what is special, including what is especially hard to bear.
SX4: The sexual Four lives feelings with full force, including physical ones. When her eyes water and burn, the boundary between allergic reaction and emotional expression easily blurs for her – the body weeps along, in a sense, whenever the longing for pure, untroubled experience once again founders on irritated reality.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that keeps its own boundary under control ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five prefers to withdraw into a controlled, low-stimulus retreat – and it is precisely the invisible, uncontrollable pollen in the air that breaks through this protection, triggering resistance that shows up as an overreaction of the mucous membrane. What cannot be observed and calculated in advance is defended against by the body as a precaution.
SO5: For the social Five, knowledge is a means of control, yet allergens can only be mastered to a limited degree, no matter how much one knows about pollen calendars and triggers. This gap between intellectual understanding and physical helplessness produces a quiet frustration that further irritates an already sensitive organism.
SX5: The sexual Five rarely opens up fully – except in intense contact with one chosen person or one chosen subject. This rare permeability in the emotional realm has a physical counterpart: when her otherwise controlled boundary-keeping momentarily relaxes, the body's immunological vigilance can likewise fall out of balance.
--- Type 6: Fear that keeps the boundary on alert ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six stockpiles knowledge and remedies against every conceivable danger – including pollen, which reliably returns every year. The precautionary vigilance with which she braces for the season is mirrored, paradoxically, in an immune system that is itself overly cautious about harmless stimuli.
SO6: Within the group, the social Six orients herself by shared rules and authorities, even when it comes to health – she conscientiously follows what doctors, forums, or family traditions recommend. Her own uncertainty about whether the reaction is normal or worrying can further fuel the allergic tension.
SX6: The sexual Six alternates between courageous confrontation of her own fears and sudden withdrawal – a pattern that repeats itself in her relationship to allergens: sometimes pollen season is defiantly ignored, sometimes avoided with excessive caution. This swing between control and surrender keeps the nervous system, and with it the mucous membranes, in a permanent state of alarm.
--- Type 7: Excess that overrides its own boundary ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven plans her comforts carefully and would rather not have a runny nose spoil the enjoyment of a beautiful spring day. Yet her tendency to quickly push aside or play down unpleasant sensations means the allergic reaction is often only treated once it can hardly be ignored anymore.
SO7: The social Seven wants to infect everyone with her lightness and has little patience for a suffering that cannot be joked away. She tends to downplay the symptoms and improvise coping strategies, rather than taking the time that a thorough regulation of the allergy would require.
SX7: The sexual Seven throws herself into new experiences with full enthusiasm, even where pollen or pet hair are unavoidable, and initially accepts the reaction as the price of admission. Only once the symptoms themselves begin to cloud the intensity of experience she craves – through swollen eyes or shortness of breath, for instance – does the allergy get taken seriously as an issue at all.
--- Type 8: Control that allows no weakness in its defenses ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight tolerates no weakness, not even her own, and responds to an allergic nose first with impatience rather than care. This refusal to pay attention to her body often lets the reaction escalate until it can no longer be pushed away and visibly undermines the very control this subtype prizes so highly.
SO8: Whoever, like the social Eight, takes on responsibility for others rarely has time to be bothered by a runny nose – it gets treated as a tiresome side issue while her real energy flows into the protector role. Only once the symptoms noticeably restrict her ability to act does she reluctantly grant them any attention.
SX8: The sexual Eight lives pure intensity and responds to physical discomfort with the same uncompromising will she brings to everything else – resistance gets fought down, not negotiated. This confrontational stance toward her own body can intensify the allergic alarm reaction rather than calm it.
--- Type 9: Self-forgetting that overlooks its own boundary ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine grows accustomed to almost anything, including a year after year recurring allergy, and happily postpones any real engagement with its triggers. This tendency toward quiet accommodation means the reaction often goes untreated for years, even though it has long been noticeably limiting daily life.
SO9: The social Nine does not want to be a burden to anyone, not even with health complaints, and often swallows sneezing and itching without complaint, so as not to disturb group harmony with her own needs. The obvious treatment – antihistamines, desensitization – thus remains conspicuously unused for a long time.
SX9: The sexual Nine merges so completely with her beloved person or environment that her own physical signals easily recede into the background – even an allergic reaction is sometimes only noticed once her partner points it out with concern. This fusion with the outside makes it harder even to notice her own boundary, let alone protect it.
Hay fever indicates where one's own boundary between inside and outside reacts too sensitively or is too poorly protected. Psychosomatic work on the allergy can help shape one's own capacity for boundary-setting – in thinking, feeling, and everyday life – more consciously, without hardening or opening up completely.

Chronic Sinusitis (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
Inflammation of the sinuses lasting weeks or months, with a feeling of pressure, a blocked nose, and impaired sense of smell.
Definition: Chronic sinusitis is diagnosed when inflammation of the sinus mucous membrane lasts longer than twelve weeks or keeps recurring. Unlike an acute cold, it does not heal on its own, because the mucous membrane stays permanently swollen, the natural drainage of secretions from the sinuses is obstructed, and mucus accumulates. Typical are a dull pressure over the forehead, cheeks, or between the eyes, permanently obstructed nasal breathing, impaired sense of smell, and thick mucus that often drains into the throat („postnasal drip“). Common causes are anatomical narrowings, nasal polyps, chronic allergies, or repeated bacterial infections that never let the mucous membrane fully settle.
Typical symptoms: Persistent pressure or pain over the forehead, cheeks, or eyes; Chronically blocked, obstructed nasal breathing; Diminished or absent sense of smell; Thick mucus draining into the throat; A feeling of pressure that worsens on bending forward; Persistent fatigue and reduced capacity
Emergency notice: In case of severe, one-sided headache with fever, visual disturbances, swelling around the eye, or confusion, seek medical help immediately (a sign of possible spread of the inflammation toward the eye or brain). In case of persistent, bloody discharge from only one side of the nose, seek medical evaluation.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
The sinuses are air-filled cavities in the skull that, in TCM, are closely tied to the lung and its Metal element – the realm that also stands for clarity, discernment, and the „letting go“ of what is no longer needed. Where mucus backs up over weeks and cannot drain, psychosomatic medicine often finds a similar backup in a figurative sense: unresolved thoughts, postponed decisions, a feeling of tightness and pressure that never clears. The dull pressure behind forehead and cheeks can thus become the physical echo of a mental inability to „breathe through“. For each of the 27 subtypes, its own pattern shows what this backup is rooted in.
--- Type 1: Anger that backs up in the head ---
SE1: The self-preservation One often carries unspoken anger over shortcomings around with her for years, without ever giving it space – an inner backup that can mirror itself in the body when secretions accumulate in the sinuses instead of draining freely. The relief that comes when the pressure finally eases often coincides exactly with the moment she allows herself a little leniency for once.
SO1: Whoever, like the social One, constantly weighs what is right and wrong carries around many unspoken judgments that are rarely voiced openly. This inner store of withheld criticism can settle in the body as persistent pressure – a head that is literally too full of what actually needs to be said.
SX1: The sexual One lives her demand for perfection with great intensity and reacts correspondingly strongly when reality does not meet her high standards. This dammed-up outrage can manifest as a chronic pressure sensation in the forehead and sinuses that only eases once the inner anger is actually voiced or productively redirected.
--- Type 2: Pride that suppresses its own needs ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two accumulates small hurts over years, accepting them while caring for others without ever putting them into words. Like secretions backing up in the sinuses because they cannot drain anywhere, this unspoken need of her own backs up too – until the pressure becomes noticeable.
SO2: For the social Two, it is only natural to be indispensable in many relationships at once – yet her own needs often remain unresolved in the process, like mucus backing up in several sinuses at the same time. Clarity about what she herself wants only arises once she allows herself to be as present for herself as she is for others.
SX2: The sexual Two merges so intensely with her beloved that her own diverging wishes often never even get formulated. This unspoken conflict between her own desire and the wish to be needed can show up as chronic pressure in the head – an inability to see her own position clearly.
--- Type 3: Achievement that leaves no room for clarity ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three keeps working efficiently even when her head has long felt heavy and dull – symptoms get organized away rather than taken seriously. This very refusal to pause can prevent the backup in the sinuses from ever truly resolving.
SO3: In front of others, the social Three wants to appear flawless and capable at all times, even with a throbbing head she hides behind a skillful facade. The constant pressure to show no weakness produces a second, invisible pressure – inside the head itself.
SX3: The sexual Three wants to shine and appear flawless even in contact with others, and happily overrides physical warning signs like a dull pressure sensation for as long as possible. Only once impaired smell or voice visibly threatens her own attractiveness does the condition finally get taken seriously.
--- Type 4: Longing that cannot discharge ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four often carries a diffuse feeling of heaviness with her that she can hardly put into words – a chronic pressure in the head fits almost seamlessly into this familiar sense of burden, without the actual cause ever being clearly named.
SO4: For the social Four, a lingering sinusitis can become a quiet symbol of a life in which much backs up without finding a real way out – a feeling of constant pressure that will not properly drain, much like her own, often unspoken, emotional fullness.
SX4: The sexual Four lives her feelings intensely, yet some longings and disappointments go unsaid and back up inside her. The dull pressure of the sinuses can physically mirror what finds no clear expression on the emotional level – too much that cannot discharge.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that reinforces its own backup ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five withdraws under strain rather than seeking contact and exchange – and it is precisely this withdrawal that can lead to a physical backup, because thoughts and feelings, too, do not drain but stay encapsulated within, much like stagnant secretion in the sinuses.
SO5: The social Five gathers knowledge in order to pass it on to select people, but holds back many of her own assessments until the right moment seems to have arrived. This holding-back can manifest as persistent pressure in the head – too much accumulated material that has not yet found its way out.
SX5: The sexual Five rarely opens up fully, usually only toward one chosen person or one chosen subject. In the meantime, a great deal backs up inside her unshared – a state that can show up physically as chronic pressure in the forehead and sinuses.
--- Type 6: Fear that backs up as pressure in the head ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six mulls persistently over possible dangers and precautions, never quite letting her own worries settle. This endless mental circling can mirror itself physically as persistent pressure in the head – a system that never fully finds relaxation.
SO6: The social Six seeks security in shared rules and authorities, but often holds back her own doubts so as not to unsettle the group. This unspoken inner uncertainty can show up as a chronic backup in the head area that only eases once trust in her own judgment grows.
SX6: The sexual Six moves between bold advances and sudden doubt, without this inner tension ever fully resolving. The shifting pressure in her head, sometimes stronger, sometimes weaker, can mirror this constant inner rollercoaster between control and letting go.
--- Type 7: Excess that plays down its own backup ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven plans her life so that unpleasant feelings get as little room as possible – a heavy head, too, gets happily played down and drowned out with the next pleasant activity, rather than being traced to its actual cause.
SO7: The social Seven prefers to keep the mood in the group light and positive, even when her own head feels heavy – her own complaints get talked down so as not to dampen others' good spirits. The unaddressed pressure thus persists, well hidden behind a smile.
SX7: The sexual Seven throws herself with full enthusiasm from one stimulus to the next and easily overhears the quieter warning signs of a slowly building pressure in the head. Only once the symptoms themselves begin to impair the intensity of experience she craves does her own health come into focus.
--- Type 8: Control that allows no pressure release ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight ignores physical complaints for as long as possible, determined to show no weakness whatsoever – a dull pressure in the head gets pushed down if need be, until it can no longer be ignored and visibly undermines the reliable capacity to act she otherwise prizes.
SO8: Whoever, like the social Eight, carries a great deal of responsibility for others rarely has time for her own health – a chronic pressure in the head gets pushed aside for as long as possible, until it becomes an unmissable burden that also limits her protector role.
SX8: The sexual Eight meets resistance, including within her own body, with the same confrontational stance she brings to everything else. Persistent pressure in the head gets fought down rather than attended to – until exhaustion eventually undermines this strategy.
--- Type 9: Self-forgetting that overrides its own backup ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine grows accustomed to almost any state, including a permanently heavy head, and happily postpones the actual clarification of its cause. So the backup in the sinuses sometimes persists for years without ever being seriously addressed.
SO9: The social Nine does not want to disturb group harmony with her own complaints and often carries a chronic pressure in the head around without complaint. Only once the impairment can no longer be overlooked does she allow herself to make her own health an issue.
SX9: The sexual Nine merges so completely with her beloved person or relationship that her own physical signals easily go unnoticed – persistent pressure in the head is often only noticed once her partner points out with concern that something is wrong.
Chronic sinusitis is a reminder of where in life a backup has formed that no longer finds a natural outlet – mentally, emotionally, or in unspoken words. Psychosomatic engagement with the feeling of pressure can help consciously recognize this backup and open paths for it, instead of permanently suppressing it.

Sleep Apnea (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep that lead to oxygen deprivation, arousal reactions, and pronounced daytime fatigue.
Definition: In obstructive sleep apnea, the muscles of the throat relax so much during sleep that the upper airway repeatedly narrows or closes completely. The result is pauses in breathing lasting from ten seconds to over a minute, often occurring dozens to hundreds of times per night, followed by brief, usually unnoticed arousal reactions with which the body restarts breathing. Those affected have no memory of these micro-arousals, yet sleep loses almost all of its restorative depth. Typical consequences are loud, irregular snoring, morning headaches, pronounced daytime fatigue, and an increased risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease. The rarer central sleep apnea, by contrast, arises from a disturbance in the brain's own breathing control.
Typical symptoms: Loud, irregular snoring with audible pauses in breathing; Abrupt nighttime startling or gasping for air; Pronounced daytime fatigue despite adequate sleep duration; Morning headaches; Difficulty concentrating and memory problems; Irritability and low mood
Emergency notice: In case of observed, prolonged pauses in breathing, bluish lips, or severe shortness of breath during sleep, seek prompt medical evaluation. Untreated sleep apnea increases the risk of microsleep while driving – with pronounced daytime fatigue, refrain from operating vehicles or machinery until an evaluation has taken place.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
In almost every healing tradition, sleep is considered the state of greatest surrender of control – the moment when the waking self lets go and gives itself over to the unconscious, to the body, to trust in the night. When, of all moments, breathing itself falters right here, it is worth asking psychosomatically where in life a similar pattern exists: a deep, mostly unconscious difficulty in truly letting go, without control – here, over one's own breath – appearing immediately at risk. For each of the 27 subtypes, its own pattern shows how this struggle between letting go and control finds expression in sleep.
--- Type 1: Control that will not let go even in sleep ---
SE1: The self-preservation One keeps everything under strict control during the day and correspondingly struggles to truly let go in sleep. The body, which functions so disciplined while awake, falls paradoxically out of step at night – as if control were failing exactly where it can least be consciously exercised.
SO1: Whoever, like the social One, carries the responsibility during the day for everything running correctly in the group finds it hard to switch off that vigilance at night as well. The breathing pauses of sleep apnea can be read as a physical picture of how much sleep, too, remains pervaded by an inner authority of control that never fully rests.
SX1: The sexual One lives tension with great intensity and often carries muscular tension in the throat and jaw into the night as well, which can further narrow the airway. The body seems reluctant to allow itself the full relaxation it would need, even at night.
--- Type 2: Pride that stays awake even in sleep ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two often stays in a kind of standby posture well into sleep, in case someone should need her during the night. This unconscious vigilance, paired with the frequent weight gain that results from constantly setting herself aside, favors, both physically and emotionally, sleep that never turns out fully relaxed.
SO2: The social Two is present for many people at once during the day and rarely truly lets go – even at night, part of her attention often stays with the needs of others. The disturbed sleep depth of apnea can physically mirror how hard it is for her to look after herself first.
SX2: The sexual Two often seeks physical closeness to her beloved even in sleep and rarely allows herself to settle entirely for herself alone. This unconscious orientation toward the other can prevent her own breath from truly flowing freely and independently during sleep.
--- Type 3: Achievement that turns sleep into a function ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three optimizes even sleep as a performance factor and struggles to experience it as a time of pure surrender. This inner tension of still having to „function“ even in sleep can go hand in hand physically with shallower, more disturbed breathing.
SO3: Whoever, like the social Three, maintains a flawless image all day often carries this tension unconsciously into the night. Loud snoring and visible breathing pauses contradict this image especially clearly – one reason the diagnosis is often delayed for a long time in this subtype.
SX3: The sexual Three wants to appear attractive even in sleep, in the presence of a partner – the thought of snoring loudly or visibly gasping for air fundamentally contradicts this aspiration. This shame can delay an honest engagement with the problem for a long time.
--- Type 4: Longing that keeps sleep restless ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four often experiences sleep disturbances as further proof of a life that feels heavier than that of others. Morning exhaustion fits almost seamlessly into a self-image in which even the night brings no genuine recovery.
SO4: For the social Four, constant daytime fatigue can become a quiet piece of evidence for how different and burdened her life is compared to others who seem effortlessly rested. Physical exhaustion thus unconsciously reinforces a feeling of separateness.
SX4: The sexual Four lives closeness and intensity with great force, including in the shared bed – and sometimes carries emotional tension into the night that shows up physically. Restless, interrupted sleep can mirror her constant struggle between longing for merging and fear of being left.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that stays watchful even in sleep ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five likes to withdraw early to conserve energy – yet even in sleep, a watchful, observing part often stays active, preventing true, complete letting go. The breathing pauses can be a physical echo of this inner distance that is never quite given up.
SO5: The social Five keeps thinking through complex matters even in the evening and rarely lets her mind fully settle. This mental activity extending deep into the night can physically make deep, relaxed breathing harder.
SX5: The sexual Five rarely opens up fully; even asleep next to a beloved person, a fine inner watchfulness often remains. This unconscious reserve can show up physically as breathing that never quite reaches its full depth.

SE6: The self-preservation Six stays in a kind of standby mode even at night, ready to react to possible dangers. This latent state of alarm in the nervous system can show up physically in restless sleep interspersed with arousal reactions.
SO6: The social Six frequently worries about the well-being of her group and carries these worries into sleep. The many brief, unnoticed arousal reactions of apnea can physically depict how hard it is to truly lay down her constant inner wakefulness.
SX6: The sexual Six moves between courageous devotion and sudden mistrust – this interplay can persist even in sleep, so the body never quite finds rest. Interrupted breathing can mirror this inner disagreement between trust and caution.

SE7: The self-preservation Seven likes to fill the day with pleasant activities and often only goes to bed late and overtired, so as not to miss out on anything. This chronic under-supply of adequate sleep can further worsen the symptoms of an existing apnea.
SO7: The social Seven wants to still appear present and entertaining even after a long, sociable evening, and often pushes tiredness aside. Only once daytime fatigue begins to slow down her own sparkling energy is the subject of sleep taken seriously.
SX7: The sexual Seven keeps seeking intense experiences even in the evening and gladly avoids rest periods. The recovery she actually needs is thereby chronically shortened, which can further intensify existing breathing problems during sleep.
--- Type 8: Control that allows no surrender in sleep ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight does not really want to give up control even in sleep and reacts correspondingly indignantly when someone tells her about loud snoring or breathing pauses. This defensive stance toward her own vulnerability frequently delays the necessary diagnosis.
SO8: Whoever, like the social Eight, carries a great deal of responsibility has little patience for nighttime complaints, which get dismissed as a tiresome side issue. Only once daytime fatigue noticeably undermines her own assertiveness is the problem taken seriously.
SX8: The sexual Eight lives intensity with full force and finds the idea of gasping helplessly for air during sleep especially unpleasant. This aversion to her own vulnerability in sleep can lead to complaints being suppressed for a long time.
--- Type 9: Self-forgetting that overrides its own sleep ---

SO9: The social Nine does not want to be a burden to anyone, not even with the request to have her own snoring medically evaluated. Daytime fatigue is rather accepted in silence than actively pursued as her own concern.
SX9: The sexual Nine merges so completely with her partner that her own physical symptoms are often only noticed once he or she raises them with concern during shared sleep. Perceiving her own exhaustion tends to be considerably harder for this subtype than perceiving it in her partner.
Sleep apnea is a reminder of how hard it can sometimes be to truly let go, even in sleep. Psychosomatic engagement with the breathing pauses can help meet one's own need for control more consciously, even at night – without replacing the necessary sleep-medicine treatment.

Pneumonia (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
Acute inflammation of lung tissue, usually caused by bacteria or viruses, with fever, cough, and shortness of breath.
Definition: Pneumonia is an acute inflammation of lung tissue, usually triggered by bacteria, less often by viruses or fungi. The pathogens invade the alveoli, which then fill with inflammatory secretion – gas exchange is impaired, and the body responds with high fever, chills, a productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. A distinction is made between community-acquired pneumonia, which arises in everyday life, and the hospital-acquired form, which often runs a more severe course. Older people, people with a weakened immune system, and people with pre-existing lung conditions are especially at risk. Unlike the chronic respiratory conditions in this category, pneumonia is an acute, potentially life-threatening event that requires prompt medical intervention.
Typical symptoms: High fever and chills; Productive cough with yellowish-green or rust-colored sputum; Increasing shortness of breath, even at rest; Stabbing pain when breathing (when the pleura is involved); Accelerated pulse and breathing rate; Pronounced weakness and confusion, especially in older people
Emergency notice: In case of high fever combined with shortness of breath, bluish lips, severe confusion, or very rapid breathing, seek emergency medical care immediately. Pneumonia can be life-threatening, especially in older or immunocompromised people, and must be treated medically without delay.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
While the chronic respiratory conditions in this category often mirror fixed patterns grown over years, pneumonia is an acute event – a body that reacts suddenly and with full force once its own defenses can no longer withstand a pathogen. In TCM, the lung is considered the organ most sensitive to outer influences, but also the seat of grief. Acute pneumonia psychosomatically often falls into phases of life in which one's own powers of resistance were already weakened by exhaustion, overload, or unprocessed grief – the pathogen meets ground that no longer has the strength to stand up to it. For each of the 27 subtypes, its own pattern shows how this exhaustion may have come about.
--- Type 1: Anger that holds out until exhaustion ---
SE1: The self-preservation One often keeps working until utter exhaustion, because pausing feels like negligence – it is precisely this exhaustion that can weaken her defenses so far that an infection can spread unhindered into the lung. Pneumonia forces the body to take the break her mind would never have permitted.
SO1: Whoever, like the social One, carries responsibility over a long time for everything running correctly in the group, rarely grants herself a genuine breather. An acute pneumonia can, in such phases, be the moment the body pulls the emergency brake, because self-care was long overdue.
SX1: The sexual One lives tension and expectation with great intensity and often ignores physical exhaustion until it can no longer be played down. A severe pneumonia can, in this constellation, become an unmistakable signal that her own uncompromising stance toward herself needs limits.
--- Type 2: Pride that overrides its own exhaustion ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two often cares for others until her own reserves of strength are used up – pneumonia hits, in such moments, an immune system already weakened by chronic self-neglect.
SO2: The social Two is there for many people at once and easily overlooks her own warning signs of exhaustion. An acute pneumonia can be the moment the body unmistakably demands to finally be cared for herself.
SX2: The sexual Two invests her entire energy in her beloved and sometimes neglects her own physical regeneration in the process. A severe illness like pneumonia can thus become the one situation in which she allows herself to actually be cared for, instead of caring for someone else.
--- Type 3: Achievement that keeps functioning until collapse ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three often keeps working even with first signs of illness, because being sidelined feels like failure. This very ignoring of early warning signs can let a harmless infection grow into a full-blown, severe pneumonia.
SO3: In front of others, the social Three wants to appear capable at all times and therefore often delays signs of illness rather than seeking timely medical treatment. A severe pneumonia forces her into a time-out she would hardly have granted herself voluntarily.
SX3: The sexual Three wants to appear attractive and strong even when ill and tends to play down initial symptoms. Only once fever and shortness of breath can no longer be masked does she admit to herself that her body urgently needs rest.
--- Type 4: Longing that exhausts its own strength ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four often experiences physical exhaustion as a familiar state and easily overlooks the transition from ordinary tiredness to a serious infection. A pneumonia can, in this shift of perception, only late reveal itself for what it is.
SO4: For the social Four, a severe illness like pneumonia can unconsciously become evidence of how much her own suffering differs from that of others. At the same time, the illness forces a rest that counteracts her otherwise often restless inner comparing with others.
SX4: The sexual Four often lives emotional exhaustion after intense relationship phases physically as well – the deep exhaustion that sets in during such phases can weaken her defenses and favor an infection that spreads into the lung.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that conceals its own weakness ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five withdraws when exhausted rather than actively seeking medical help, and often observes her own symptoms for a long time before acting. This delay can allow an emerging pneumonia to progress unhindered.
SO5: The social Five researches signs of illness thoroughly before turning to medical help – valuable time that can be missing with a rapidly worsening pneumonia. Trusting swift medical action tends to be harder for this subtype than her own study of the facts.
SX5: The sexual Five truly opens up to only a few people and tends to conceal physical weakness as much as possible. A severe pneumonia can interrupt this withdrawal, because physical distress outweighs her habitual protective mechanism of reserve.
--- Type 6: Fear that wears down its own strength ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six usually takes conscientious care of her health, yet ongoing worry and tension can exhaust her defenses over time. A pneumonia then meets an immune system already weakened by chronic inner alarm.
SO6: The social Six frequently worries intensely about the well-being of others and sets her own warning signs aside in the process. An acute pneumonia can, in this constellation, be the moment care must finally be directed at herself.
SX6: The sexual Six lives in constant alarm between trust and mistrust, which can over time exhaust the nervous system and, with it, her defenses. A severe illness can thus also be an expression of an inner reserve used up over a long time.
--- Type 7: Excess that plays down its own exhaustion ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven happily plays down first signs of illness with the next pleasant activity, instead of granting herself the necessary rest. This avoidance of the unpleasant can let a harmless infection grow into a pneumonia that needs to be taken seriously.
SO7: The social Seven does not want to dampen the good mood even while ill and frequently delays her own symptoms so as not to burden others. Only a severe illness like pneumonia forces her into the pause she otherwise only reluctantly takes.
SX7: The sexual Seven keeps throwing herself into new experiences, even when her body has long been asking for rest, because pausing feels like a loss. An acute pneumonia interrupts this pull toward intensity with unmistakable clarity.
--- Type 8: Control that denies its own exhaustion ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight deliberately ignores signs of illness in order to show no weakness, and often keeps working until exhaustion. A developing pneumonia is therefore frequently only recognized once it has already reached a serious extent.
SO8: Whoever, like the social Eight, carries responsibility for others gladly puts her own health last, until her body leaves her no other choice. A severe pneumonia forces a surrender to her own vulnerability that is especially hard for this subtype.
SX8: The sexual Eight meets even illness first with confrontation rather than giving in – symptoms get fought down rather than attended to. Only once a pneumonia massively restricts her physical strength does she reluctantly allow herself to accept help.
--- Type 9: Self-forgetting that overlooks its own exhaustion ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine happily postpones engaging with first signs of illness and hopes everything will resolve on its own. A worsening pneumonia can, unfortunately, thus be recognized as serious only late.
SO9: The social Nine does not want to be a burden to anyone and often conceals her own signs of illness, so as not to disturb the daily lives of others. Only a severe pneumonia makes clear that her own health deserves just as much attention as that of others.
SX9: The sexual Nine merges so completely with her beloved that her own physical warning signs easily go unnoticed. A pneumonia in this subtype is sometimes only noticed once her partner intervenes and insists on medical evaluation.
Pneumonia is always an acute event that requires medical treatment. Seen psychosomatically, it can at the same time point to a phase in which one's own powers of resistance were already exhausted before the infection – an occasion to take one's own exhaustion seriously, rather than allowing it only once the body has no choice left.

Hyperventilation Syndrome (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
Sudden bouts of breathing too fast and too deep, usually triggered by acute anxiety or chronic stress, with tingling, dizziness, and tightness.
Definition: In hyperventilation syndrome, the affected person breathes noticeably faster and deeper than the body needs for its current oxygen demand. This causes too much carbon dioxide to be exhaled, shifting the blood's acid-base balance, and leads to symptoms such as tingling in the hands, feet, and around the mouth, dizziness, tightness in the chest, a racing heart, and, in pronounced cases, cramping of the hands (carpopedal spasm). Triggers are usually acute anxiety, panic, or ongoing psychological stress; organic causes must, however, be medically ruled out before the diagnosis is made. Unlike asthma, the problem here is not narrowing of the airways but a misregulation of breathing depth and rate itself.
Typical symptoms: Fast, shallow or noticeably deep breathing; Tingling or numbness in the hands, feet, and around the mouth; Dizziness and lightheadedness; Tightness or pressure in the chest; Racing heart and trembling; In pronounced cases, cramping of the hands (carpopedal spasm)
Emergency notice: On first occurrence, or with additional symptoms such as severe chest pain, one-sided weakness, or altered consciousness, seek emergency medical care immediately to reliably rule out other, more serious causes. Only after a medically confirmed diagnosis should breathing into a bag or into cupped hands be used as a self-help measure.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Breathing is the only vital bodily function that is both involuntary and voluntary at once – it runs automatically, yet can be consciously influenced at any moment. It is precisely at this interface between conscious and unconscious that hyperventilation syndrome takes hold: acute fear or pent-up stress that finds no other expression reaches directly into breathing and throws its natural rhythm off balance. Unlike the chronic conditions in this category, what shows up here is usually not a pattern grown over years but an acute overload of the nervous system that discharges immediately in the body. For each of the 27 subtypes, its own pattern shows where this acute overload has its origin.
--- Type 1: Anger that suddenly discharges through the breath ---
SE1: The self-preservation One usually keeps anger and tension under disciplined control, until the inner pressure eventually finds no other way out than through breathing. A hyperventilation attack can thus be the moment her otherwise so taut self-control briefly loses the upper hand.
SO1: Whoever, like the social One, constantly watches over everything running correctly, easily slips into a spiral of tension under sudden overload that transfers directly to her breathing. The body reacts exactly where the mind can no longer maintain control.
SX1: The sexual One lives outrage at imperfection with great intensity, and when this intensity finds no outlet, it can discharge in an acute hyperventilation attack – the body, in a sense, breathes off the pent-up arousal that was not allowed to express itself in words.
--- Type 2: Pride that must not show sudden fear ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two sets her own needs aside for so long that the inner pressure eventually can no longer be held – a hyperventilation attack can, in such moments, be the point at which the body unmistakably signals that the limit of self-sacrifice has been reached.
SO2: The social Two tries to be indispensable to many people at once and, under overload, easily slips into a state of inner breathlessness that discharges physically as actual breathlessness.
SX2: The sexual Two often fears the loss of her beloved so intensely that acute relationship anxiety can transfer directly onto her breathing. A hyperventilation attack can, in this constellation, be a direct physical expression of an overwhelming fear of loss.
--- Type 3: Achievement that collapses under acute pressure ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three drives herself to high achievement and often ignores her own limits of strain, until her body abruptly forces a pause with an acute attack. Breathing becomes the one uncontrollable authority in a life otherwise ruled by control.
SO3: In front of others, the social Three wants to appear composed at all times, which is why a visible hyperventilation attack is especially embarrassing for her – yet it is precisely the effort to show no weakness that can build inner tension so far that it discharges right there.
SX3: The sexual Three stands under constant pressure to shine in contact with others and can barely compensate for this pressure under heavy stress. An acute attack can be the moment her maintained brilliance briefly collapses.
--- Type 4: Longing that suddenly overwhelms the breath ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four often experiences feelings with great intensity without finding a reliable way to regulate them. A hyperventilation attack can be the physical expression of an emotional flooding for which everyday life offers no other channel.
SO4: For the social Four, the feeling of being alone with her own emotional intensity can, in acute moments of overload, transfer directly onto her breathing – the body reacts to an emotional loneliness that finds no verbal expression.
SX4: The sexual Four lives longing and despair with full force, and when these feelings overwhelm her in an intense relationship situation, the emotional overwhelm can discharge in an acute attack in which breath can no longer keep pace with the intensity of feeling.
--- Type 5: Withdrawal that collapses under sudden closeness ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five usually keeps feelings at a distance and only reacts physically once the inner tension can no longer be controlled. A hyperventilation attack can thus be the rare moment in which her otherwise so composed distance collapses.
SO5: The social Five frequently analyzes burdens mentally rather than processing them emotionally, and can, under sudden overload, slip into a state in which the mind loses control – a state that transfers directly onto her breathing.
SX5: The sexual Five rarely opens up fully, and when strong feelings nonetheless break through in an intense bond, this unfamiliar emotional permeability can overwhelm her body and discharge in an acute attack.
--- Type 6: Fear that discharges directly through the breath ---

SE7: The self-preservation Seven usually skillfully sidesteps unpleasant feelings, but when this avoidance hits its limits, the pent-up fear can discharge in an acute attack – the one moment in which her otherwise so nimble evasion no longer works.
SO7: The social Seven happily plays down her own worries with optimism, but under heavy pressure this facade can crack, and the withheld fear discharges directly through her breathing.
SX7: The sexual Seven seeks intensity to stay ahead of unpleasant feelings, but when a situation overwhelms her anyway, sudden confrontation with her own fear can trigger an acute hyperventilation attack.

SX8: The sexual Eight usually meets threat with immediate confrontation, but when a situation spins out of control and even this strategy fails, the pent-up arousal can discharge in an acute attack.
--- Type 9: Self-forgetting that suddenly shows fear ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine usually skillfully suppresses uncomfortable tensions, but when too much unspoken has accumulated, this inner tension can discharge suddenly and uncontrolled through her breathing.
SO9: The social Nine often maintains peace in the group at the cost of her own tension, which builds up unnoticed over a long time. An acute hyperventilation attack can be the moment this suppressed tension becomes impossible to overlook.
SX9: The sexual Nine merges so completely with her beloved relationship that her own fears are rarely named – when this suppressed fear breaks through nonetheless, it sometimes happens abruptly, in the form of an acute attack that breaks through her otherwise so merged calm.
Hyperventilation syndrome is a reminder that acute inner tension, when it finds no other expression, can discharge directly through breathing. Psychosomatic work on it can help notice fear and stress earlier and more consciously, instead of allowing them only in an acute attack.

Chronic Tonsillitis (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
Recurring or persistent inflammation of the tonsils with a sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and swollen lymph nodes.
Definition: Chronic tonsillitis is diagnosed when the tonsils are repeatedly acutely inflamed or remain permanently enlarged, reddened, and coated with whitish deposits. The tonsils belong to the lymphatic defense system at the entrance of the mouth and throat and normally filter out pathogens before they penetrate deeper into the body. In chronic inflammation, however, they themselves become permanently overloaded, lose their filtering function, and become the starting point of recurring infections. Typical complaints are persistent sore throat, difficulty swallowing, bad breath, and swollen neck lymph nodes. With frequently recurring acute flare-ups (several times a year), surgical removal of the tonsils is often considered.
Typical symptoms: Persistent or recurring sore throat; Difficulty swallowing; Whitish deposits or plugs of pus on the tonsils; Bad breath; Swollen, tender neck lymph nodes; Mild, persistent feeling of illness and fatigue
Emergency notice: In case of very severe difficulty swallowing with drooling, muffled speech, marked one-sided swelling in the throat, or shortness of breath, seek emergency medical care immediately (a sign of a possible tonsillar abscess). In case of high fever lasting several days, seek medical evaluation.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
The tonsils sit at a symbolically significant place: the entrance where it is decided what is let into the body and what is fended off – and, at the same time, right at the exit of the voice, the place where words leave the body. Psychosomatically, the throat is traditionally associated with what wants to be said but is not allowed to be said, or cannot be said. A chronically inflamed tonsil can thus be read as a place where withheld words, suppressed objection, or a constant swallowing of too much settle physically. For each of the 27 subtypes, its own pattern shows which words are especially often swallowed here.
--- Type 1: Anger that gets swallowed ---
SE1: The self-preservation One often holds back sharp criticism, because an open accusation does not fit her image of composure. This constantly swallowed correction can settle physically in a throat that stays chronically irritated and inflamed.
SO1: Whoever, like the social One, constantly watches over everything running correctly, often suppresses the impulse to correct others directly, so as not to endanger the group's harmony. Withheld lessons can make themselves noticeable as a persistent irritation in the throat.
SX1: The sexual One lives outrage intensely, yet holds some of it back especially in close relationships, so as not to be seen as overly critical. This withholding of sharp words at moments of greatest emotional closeness can chronically burden the throat.

SO2: The social Two often holds back her own exhaustion or disappointment, in order to keep being seen as a reliable support for many. What is not allowed to be voiced backs up in the throat, both figuratively and literally.
SX2: The sexual Two often conceals her own doubts about the relationship, out of fear of endangering closeness to her beloved. These withheld truths can manifest as persistent irritation in the throat.

SE3: The self-preservation Three usually swallows her own exhaustion, in order to keep appearing capable – words like „I can't manage this right now“ rarely get voiced, but stay stuck in the throat.

SX3: The sexual Three wants to appear radiant at all times in contact with others and often swallows her own disappointments rather than naming them. These unspoken feelings can permanently burden the throat.

SO4: For the social Four, much of her own experience remains unsaid, because she fears meeting incomprehension with it. What inwardly seems too special or too vulnerable to say out loud can settle as a persistent burden in the throat.
SX4: The sexual Four lives longing with great intensity, yet sometimes conceals her most vulnerable wishes out of fear of rejection. This withholding of the deepest truth can chronically irritate the throat.

SE5: The self-preservation Five usually prefers to hold her own thoughts back rather than voice them unprompted. This restraint, trained over years, can settle physically in a throat that far too often does not get to speak.

SX5: The sexual Five rarely opens up fully and often conceals precisely her most intense thoughts and feelings. This rare but intense restraint can show up physically as recurring throat infections.

Chronic tonsillitis is a reminder of where words were swallowed rather than spoken over an extended time. Psychosomatic engagement with the throat can help give one's own unspoken part more conscious room and voice.

Chronic Cough (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
A cough lasting more than eight weeks without an acute infection, often without a clear single cause and with considerable impact on daily life.
Definition: Chronic cough is diagnosed when it persists for more than eight weeks without an acute infection being present. Unlike the productive cough of bronchitis or the fit-like cough of asthma, the cause of chronic cough often remains unclear at first – possible causes include postnasal drip from the sinuses, reflux of stomach acid into the esophagus, a hidden form of asthma, medication side effects, or a not-yet-recognized irritation of the airways. In a relevant proportion of cases, no clear organic cause is found despite thorough diagnostics – this is then called idiopathic chronic cough. The cough itself often becomes an independent, self-reinforcing reflex: the constant mechanical irritation from coughing further irritates the mucous membrane and provokes renewed urge to cough.
Typical symptoms: Persistent, often dry cough lasting more than eight weeks; A scratchy or tickling sensation in the throat as a trigger; Worsening of the cough with cold, speaking, or laughing; Exhaustion from disturbed nighttime sleep; Sore muscles in the chest and abdomen from frequent coughing; Occasional hoarseness
Emergency notice: In case of chronic cough with blood in the sputum, unintended weight loss, night sweats, or increasing shortness of breath, seek prompt medical evaluation to rule out more serious causes. A newly appearing chronic cough should always be medically examined.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Coughing is originally a protective reflex that clears the airways of foreign bodies or secretion – a sudden, forceful expulsion of air. When this reflex, however, takes on a life of its own over weeks and months without a clear outer cause being identifiable, it is worth asking psychosomatically what this recurring, abrupt expulsion might still stand for. Coughing interrupts a conversation, buys a brief pause, draws attention to itself without requiring words – a nonverbal channel for something that finds no other expression. For each of the 27 subtypes, its own pattern shows what this cough can stand in for when no purely organic cause is found.
--- Type 1: Anger that discharges as a cough ---
SE1: The self-preservation One usually suppresses anger consistently, and a dry, recurring cough can show up as a small, involuntary valve for exactly this withheld resentment – a brief, controlled outburst where an open accusation is forbidden.
SO1: Whoever, like the social One, constantly watches over the correctness of processes, sometimes coughs exactly when a correction is on the tip of her tongue but stays unsaid. The cough can thus become an audible but verbally consequence-free sign of inner disagreement.
SX1: The sexual One usually lives anger with force, yet sometimes holds it back in close personal contact. A chronic cough can, in such moments, become a substitute, brief outburst that at least partly discharges the withheld intensity.
--- Type 2: Pride that signals needs through coughing ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two rarely reports her own exhaustion directly and instead lets a lingering cough speak for her – an involuntary signal that something is wrong, without having to openly demand her own needs.

Irritable Bowel Syndrome (Psychosomatics Register · Digestive System)
Recurring abdominal pain and altered bowel habits with no detectable organic cause – the gut reacts oversensitively to stimuli of every kind.
Definition: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a chronic, functional disorder of the gut in which recurring abdominal pain or cramping occurs together with altered bowel habits – diarrhea, constipation, or an alternation between the two – without any organic cause such as inflammation, ulcer, or tumor being found on examination. The diagnosis is made when symptoms have persisted for at least three months and other conditions have been ruled out. Characteristic is an increased sensitivity of the gut's nerves (visceral hypersensitivity) as well as a close coupling to the autonomic nervous system: stress, excitement, and emotional tension often worsen symptoms immediately, while the gut tends to settle during calm, relaxed phases.
Typical symptoms: Recurring, cramp-like abdominal pain that often improves after a bowel movement; Bloating and a feeling of fullness; Diarrhea, constipation, or an alternation between the two; Mucus in the stool; A feeling of incomplete emptying; Marked worsening of symptoms with stress or emotional strain
Emergency notice: In case of blood in the stool, unintended weight loss, nighttime pain that wakes you from sleep, fever, or first onset of symptoms after age 50, seek prompt medical evaluation – these warning signs argue against pure IBS and must be checked to rule out other causes.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
Research has long called the gut the „second brain“ – via the gut-brain axis it stands in direct, two-way exchange with the central nervous system, and a large share of the body's own messenger substances for mood and tension are produced in the gut itself. In TCM, a harmonious interplay of Liver and Spleen is considered the precondition for calm digestion: when Liver Qi stagnates through withheld anger or unresolved tension, it „invades“ the Spleen and disrupts its task of processing food in an orderly way. Psychosomatic medicine often reads IBS as a gut that must literally digest what the mind cannot process – every unresolved tension gets passed directly along to it. For each of the 27 subtypes, its own pattern shows what kind of tension especially often lands in the belly.

SO1: Whoever, like the social One, constantly watches over the correctness of things, carries around a great deal of withheld outrage over wrongs that is rarely voiced directly. This chronically digested criticism can show up as recurring abdominal cramps that arise exactly when something is once again felt to be wrong but left unaddressed.
SX1: The sexual One lives her demand for improvement in the relationship with great intensity – precisely in moments of escalation, when criticism must be held back, this tension can show up as an acute, episodic cramp in the belly, rather than as an even, ongoing strain.

Acid Reflux / Heartburn (GERD) (Psychosomatics Register · Digestive System)
When stomach acid keeps flowing back into the esophagus, leaving a burning sensation that cannot permanently be swallowed away.
Definition: In gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), acidic stomach contents repeatedly flow back into the esophagus because the sphincter between esophagus and stomach no longer seals reliably. The sensitive esophageal lining, which unlike the stomach lining is not built to withstand contact with acid, responds with irritation and inflammation. Reflux is favored by excess weight, certain foods (fatty, spicy, coffee, alcohol), smoking, stress, and a hiatal hernia. Left untreated, the chronic irritation can lead to changes in the lining (Barrett's esophagus) that raise the risk of esophageal cancer – an important reason to have persistent heartburn medically evaluated.
Typical symptoms: Burning sensation behind the breastbone (heartburn), often worse after eating or when lying down; Acid regurgitation, sometimes reaching the throat; Difficulty swallowing or a lump-in-the-throat feeling; Chronic cough or hoarseness, especially in the morning; A sense of pressure or nausea in the upper abdomen; Tooth damage from repeated acid exposure
Emergency notice: In case of difficulty swallowing combined with unintended weight loss, blood in vomit, or black, tarry stool, seek medical evaluation immediately. Burning chest pain can also be a symptom of a heart attack – when in doubt, especially with radiation into the arm or jaw, call emergency services immediately.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
In TCM, an upward-striving, „rebellious“ movement of Stomach Qi is considered a cause of heartburn and regurgitation – normally Stomach Qi is meant to flow downward, so that food takes its path downward too. Emotionally, this reversal is often linked to withheld anger, frustration, or resentment that finds no other outlet and instead literally comes back up. Psychosomatic medicine often reads reflux as the picture of something that should actually have been swallowed and closed off, but keeps forcing its way back up – an anger, a hurt, or a conflict that cannot be finally digested. Stomach Ulcer (Psychosomatics Register · Digestive System)
When the protective stomach lining is damaged so severely that the body's own acid begins to injure itself.
Definition: A stomach ulcer (gastric ulcer) develops when the protective mucous layer of the stomach is damaged so extensively that the aggressive stomach acid attacks the tissue beneath it. The most common cause is infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which weakens the lining's protective barrier; regular use of certain pain relievers (NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or aspirin), heavy smoking, and alcohol consumption also favor its development. Contrary to earlier assumptions, chronic stress alone is rarely the sole cause, but it can further weaken the lining and delay healing. Left untreated, a stomach ulcer can bleed or, in rare cases, break through the stomach wall (perforation) – both serious, potentially life-threatening complications.
Typical symptoms: Boring or burning pain in the upper abdomen, often related to eating; Nausea and fullness after eating; Loss of appetite and unintended weight loss; Waking at night due to abdominal pain; Heartburn and acid regurgitation; Paleness and exhaustion from chronic, mild blood loss
Emergency notice: In case of sudden, severe abdominal pain with a board-like rigid abdomen, vomiting blood (bright red or coffee-ground-like), or black, tarry stool, call emergency services immediately – these are signs of bleeding or a perforated ulcer and constitute a life-threatening emergency.
Every person can develop any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but a psychosomatic interpretive offering – patterns that stand out in practice, but never a substitute for seeing a doctor or licensed alternative practitioner.
